questions.q: Stokes' law gives drag on a small sphere as F = 6πηrv. What are the SI units of the viscosity η?
o: kg·m/s
That is momentum; it treats η as F × time.
N/m²
That is pressure; the velocity term contributes an extra second.
kg/(m·s)
Correct: η = F/(rv) = (kg·m/s²)/(m·m/s) = kg/(m·s), i.e., Pa·s.
kg/s
Divides force by velocity only, ignoring the radius.
questions.note: η is often written Pa·s.
questions.x: Rearrange Stokes' law so η = F/(6πrv). The 6π has no units, so η = N ÷ (m·m/s) = (kg·m/s²)·s/m² = kg/(m·s), which is the same as Pa·s. N/m² is tempting, but it leaves out the extra second that comes from dividing by velocity.

questions.q: Vector A is 3 m east and vector B is 4 m north. What is A − B?
o: 5 m, pointing north of east
That is A + B; subtracting B reverses its direction.
5 m, pointing south of east
Correct: A − B = A + (−B) = 3 m east + 4 m south; magnitude 5 m.
1 m, pointing east
Subtracts magnitudes, which only works for parallel vectors.
7 m, pointing south of east
Adds magnitudes instead of combining perpendicular components.
questions.note: Subtracting a vector = adding its reverse.
questions.x: To subtract a vector, add its reverse: A − B = A + (−B). Here that is 3 m east plus 4 m south. The legs are perpendicular, so the magnitude is 5 m, pointing south of east. A + B has the same magnitude but points north of east, so the direction is what tells them apart.

questions.q: An object is dropped from rest. What is the ratio of the distance it falls during the 2nd second to the distance during the 1st second?
o: Assumes distance per second grows linearly with time.
Compares total distance after 2 s (20 m) to the 1st second (5 m).
Assumes constant speed.
Correct: 5 m in the 1st second; 20 − 5 = 15 m in the 2nd; 15/5 = 3.
questions.note: Distances in successive seconds go 1 : 3 : 5 : 7.
questions.x: In free fall, distance grows as t², so the totals after 1 s and 2 s are 5 m and 20 m. The 2nd second covers 20 − 5 = 15 m, which is three times the 1st. In general, distances in successive equal intervals go in the odd-number ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7.

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight down at 10 m/s from a 15 m ledge. What is its speed just before hitting the ground (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: About 17 m/s
Ignores the initial 10 m/s (that is a drop from rest).
20 m/s
25 m/s
Adds the 10 m/s initial speed to the 15 m height as if they were like quantities.
30 m/s
Counts the 10 m/s throw twice (20 + 10): the throw speed is already inside v² = 100 + 300.
questions.note: Speeds add in quadrature in v² = v₀² + 2ad, not linearly.
questions.x: Use v² = v₀² + 2ad: 100 + 2(10)(15) = 400, so v = 20 m/s. Energy gives the same result. Speeds combine through their squares, so you cannot just add 10 m/s to the speed of a drop from rest (√300 ≈ 17 m/s).

questions.q: A ball is kicked at 20 m/s at 30° above level ground. Approximately how far away does it land?
o: Correct: flight time 2 s; vₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m/s; 17.3 × 2 ≈ 35 m.
Multiplies the vertical component (10 m/s) by the flight time.
Uses the full 20 m/s as the horizontal speed.
Uses only the time to reach the peak (1 s).
questions.x: The vertical component (10 m/s) sets the flight time: 1 s up and 1 s down, so 2 s in total. The horizontal component, 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m/s, sets the distance: 17.3 × 2 ≈ 35 m. Using the full launch speed as the horizontal speed overestimates the range.

questions.q: Compared with the ideal (no-drag) case, how does air resistance affect the launch angle that gives maximum range on level ground?
o: The optimal angle rises above 45°
Higher arcs spend more time in the air and lose more to drag.
The optimal angle stays exactly 45°
45° is optimal only without drag.
The optimal angle becomes 90°
A vertical launch has zero range.
The optimal angle drops below 45°
Correct: drag punishes long, high flights, favoring a lower trajectory.
questions.x: Without drag, the range is greatest at 45°. Drag removes energy the whole time the ball is moving, so high, long flights lose the most. A lower, faster trajectory spends less time in the air, so the best angle falls below 45°. That is why real-world throws and kicks often peak around 35–40°.

questions.q: A horse pulls a cart, and by Newton's third law the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. Why can the horse and cart still accelerate forward?
o: The horse pulls slightly harder than the cart pulls back
Third-law forces are always exactly equal.
The paired forces act on different objects, and the ground pushes the horse forward
Correct: third-law pairs never cancel on one body; ground friction on the hooves drives the system.
Third-law forces cancel only when objects are at rest
Third-law pairs are equal and opposite in all cases.
The cart's reaction force is delayed by its inertia
Third-law forces are simultaneous.
questions.note: Trap: action–reaction forces act on different objects.
questions.x: Third-law pairs are equal and opposite, but they act on different objects, so they never cancel each other. Whether the horse moves depends on the net force on the horse alone: the ground's forward friction on its hooves is larger than the cart's backward pull. Thinking the horse pulls 'harder' is the classic misconception.

questions.q: Masses of 3 kg and 5 kg hang on opposite sides of a frictionless, massless pulley. What is their acceleration (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: 4.0 m/s²
Divides the 20 N weight difference by the heavier mass only, not the total mass.
Uses the heavier weight (50 N) instead of the difference.
10 m/s²
Treats the heavier mass as if in free fall.
2.5 m/s²
questions.note: Atwood: a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂).
questions.x: Treat both masses as one system. The net driving force is the difference in weights, (5 − 3) × 10 = 20 N, and it accelerates the total mass of 8 kg: a = 2.5 m/s². Dividing by only one mass forgets that both masses move together.

questions.q: Masses of 2 kg and 6 kg hang over a frictionless, massless pulley. What is the string tension (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: That is the 2 kg weight; tension must exceed it to accelerate that mass up.
That is the 6 kg weight; tension must be less to let it accelerate down.
Averages the two weights instead of applying F = ma.
questions.x: First, a = (6 − 2)(10)/8 = 5 m/s². For the 2 kg mass accelerating upward, T − 20 = 2 × 5, so T = 30 N. The answer must lie between the two weights: above 20 N to lift the lighter mass and below 60 N so the heavier one can fall.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. What is the Newton's third-law partner of Earth's gravitational pull on the book?
o: The book's gravitational pull on Earth
Correct: third-law pairs are the same type of force between the same two objects.
The table's normal force on the book
Equal and opposite here, but it's a different force type acting on the same object.
The book's push on the table
That is the partner of the normal force.
The table's weight
That involves Earth and the table, not the book.
questions.note: Third-law pairs: same interaction, two different objects.
questions.x: A third-law pair is two sides of one interaction: if A pulls on B, B pulls on A with the same type of force. Earth pulls the book gravitationally, so the book pulls Earth gravitationally. The normal force is equal and opposite here, but it acts on the same object and is a different force, so it is not the pair.

questions.q: A 10 kg box sits on a floor with μs = 0.4. A 25 N horizontal push does not move it. What is the static friction force (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: That is the maximum possible static friction, not the actual value.
0 N
Friction must oppose the push for the box to stay at rest.
Correct: static friction matches the applied force up to its maximum (40 N).
Subtracts push from the maximum; friction simply balances the push.
questions.note: Trap: μsN is a ceiling, not the value.
questions.x: Static friction is only as large as it needs to be to stop sliding, up to the limit μsN (40 N here). A 25 N push is below that limit, so friction is exactly 25 N in the opposite direction and the box stays still. Plugging in μsN when the box is not about to slip is the trap.

questions.q: Why do anti-lock brakes typically shorten a car's stopping distance?
o: They increase the normal force on the tires
ABS doesn't change the car's weight on the road.
They convert kinetic friction into rolling resistance
Rolling resistance is tiny and wouldn't stop the car faster.
They raise μk by heating the tires
ABS works by preventing lockup, not by heating.
They keep tires rolling, so static rather than kinetic friction acts
Correct: μs > μk, so the maximum braking force is larger.
questions.x: A wheel that is rolling without skidding grips the road with static friction. A locked, skidding wheel slides with kinetic friction. Because μs > μk, ABS keeps the wheels just short of locking, which lets the car brake with a larger maximum friction force. Steering control is also kept.

questions.q: Two identical blocks slide from rest down frictionless ramps of the same height, one steep and one shallow. Which statement is correct?
o: Both arrive at the same time with the same speed
The shallow ramp is longer and has smaller acceleration.
The steep-ramp block arrives first, and both have the same final speed
Correct: final speed = √(2gh) for both; the steep ramp has larger acceleration and shorter path.
The steep-ramp block arrives first with greater speed
Speed depends only on height drop.
The shallow-ramp block arrives first
It travels farther with less acceleration.
questions.x: With no friction, energy conservation gives v = √(2gh) at the bottom for any ramp of the same height. The steep ramp has a larger acceleration (g sin θ) and a shorter path, so its block arrives first. The final speed depends only on height, while the time depends on the ramp's shape.

questions.q: A wheelchair ramp rises 1 m for every 12 m of horizontal run. Ignoring friction, about what force along the ramp is needed to push a 100 kg person and chair up at constant speed?
o: That is the full weight, needed only for a vertical lift.
About 83 N
Correct: sin θ ≈ 1/12 for a gentle slope; 1000 N × 1/12 ≈ 83 N.
Multiplies the weight by 12 instead of dividing.
About 500 N
Uses sin 30°; the ramp is far shallower.
questions.x: For gentle slopes, sin θ ≈ tan θ = rise/run = 1/12. The push needed at constant speed is mg sin θ ≈ 1000/12 ≈ 83 N. A shallow ramp trades force for distance: the work mgh is the same, but it is spread over a path about 12 times longer.

questions.q: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. In what direction does its acceleration point?
o: Along the velocity, tangent to the path
A tangential component would change the speed.
Away from the center
Centrifugal force is a fictitious force in the rotating frame.
It has no acceleration
Changing direction means changing velocity.
Toward the center of the circle
Correct: centripetal acceleration changes the direction of velocity.
questions.x: In uniform circular motion, the speed stays the same but the direction keeps changing, so the velocity changes. The acceleration points toward the center (centripetal), perpendicular to the velocity, and has magnitude v²/r. Centrifugal force is not a real force; it appears only when you analyze from inside the rotating frame.

questions.q: A car crosses the top of a circular hill of radius 40 m at 20 m/s. What is the normal force from the road on the car?
o: Equal to the car's weight
True only at very low speed or on level road.
Twice the car's weight
That would be at the bottom of a dip, not the top of a hill.
Zero
Correct: v²/r = 400/40 = 10 m/s² = g, so gravity alone supplies the centripetal force.
Half the car's weight
That would require v²/r = g/2.
questions.note: At a hilltop, N = m(g − v²/r).
questions.x: At the top of a hill, the net downward force must supply the centripetal force: mg − N = mv²/r. Here v²/r = 400/40 = 10 m/s² = g, so N = 0, and the car is just about to leave the road. A normal force that grows above the weight happens at the bottom of a dip, where N = m(g + v²/r).

questions.q: A ball whirled on a string moves in a horizontal circle. If the string snaps, what path does the ball initially follow (seen from above)?
o: A straight line tangent to the circle
Correct: with no centripetal force, it continues with its instantaneous velocity.
A straight line radially outward
No outward force exists; that is the centrifugal misconception.
A continued circular path
Circular motion needs a centripetal force.
A spiral outward
With no horizontal force, the path is straight.
questions.x: Circular motion continues only while a centripetal force keeps bending the path. When the string snaps, that force is gone, and by Newton's first law the ball moves in a straight line along its velocity at that moment, which is tangent to the circle. There was never an outward force to throw it radially outward.

questions.q: What is the minimum speed a car needs at the top of a vertical loop of radius 10 m to stay on the track (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: 0 m/s
A stopped car would fall off the top of the loop.
10 m/s
Correct: at minimum speed N = 0, so mg = mv²/r and v = √(gr) = 10 m/s.
About 14 m/s
Uses √(2gr), an energy result.
Uses gr without the square root.
questions.x: At the top of the loop, gravity and the normal force both point toward the center: mg + N = mv²/r. The lowest speed is when the track just stops pushing (N = 0), so v = √(gr) = √100 = 10 m/s. Any slower and gravity pulls the car into a tighter curve than the track, so it falls away.

questions.q: A car rounds a flat curve of radius 50 m where μs = 0.5. What is the maximum speed without skidding (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: About 16 m/s
Correct: μsg = v²/r, so v = √(0.5 × 10 × 50) = √250 ≈ 16 m/s.
25 m/s
Uses μsr = 25 without the square root and without g.
5 m/s
Uses √(μsr) without g.
Forgets the square root.
questions.note: Max speed on a flat curve is independent of mass.
questions.x: On a flat curve, static friction provides the centripetal force, so the most it can supply is μsmg = mv²/r. Mass cancels: v_max = √(μsgr) = √250 ≈ 16 m/s. Static friction applies because the tires are not sliding sideways, and leaving out g or the square root gives the wrong units.

questions.q: At what distance from Earth's center is the gravitational acceleration one-ninth of its surface value? (R = Earth's radius)
o: 9R
Assumes g ∝ 1/r.
Takes the square root of 3 instead of 9.
Squares the factor instead of taking its root.
3R
Correct: g ∝ 1/r², so 1/9 requires r = 3R.
questions.x: Formula: g = GM/r². Variables: at the surface r = R, so g₀ = GM/R²; we want g = g₀/9. Substitution: GM/r² = (1/9)·GM/R², so r² = 9R² and r = 3R. Check: g = GM/(3R)² = GM/(9R²) = g₀/9. Answer: 3R, which is 2R above the surface (r is measured from Earth's center). Using 9R treats gravity as though it fell off as 1/r.

questions.q: A uniform 4 m beam weighing 200 N rests on supports at each end. A 400 N person stands 1 m from the left end. What force does the left support exert?
o: That is the right support's force.
Correct: torques about the right end: L(4) = 200(2) + 400(3), so L = 400 N.
Splits the total 600 N equally.
That is the total load on both supports.
questions.x: Taking torques about the right support removes that unknown. The beam's weight acts at its center, 2 m from the right end, and the person is 3 m away: L × 4 = 200 × 2 + 400 × 3, so L = 400 N. As a check, the forces must add to 600 N, so R = 200 N. The person stands nearer the left, so that support carries more.

questions.q: A 4 kg lamp hangs from two strings, each making 60° with the horizontal ceiling. What is the tension in each string (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Splits the weight equally, ignoring the angle.
Assigns the full weight to each string.
About 23 N
Correct: 2T sin 60° = 40 N, so T = 40/1.73 ≈ 23 N.
About 46 N
Divides by sin 60° without splitting between strings.
questions.x: Each string pulls upward with T sin 60°, and together they must hold up the 40 N weight: 2T sin 60° = 40, so T ≈ 23 N. Each tension is more than half the weight, because part of each pull is horizontal and cancels the other string's horizontal pull. Shallower strings would need even more tension.

questions.q: A spring (k = 200 N/m) is already stretched 0.1 m. How much additional work stretches it to 0.2 m?
o: 1 J
That is the work for the first 0.1 m only.
3 J
4 J
That is the total work from 0 to 0.2 m.
2 J
Assumes each 0.1 m costs the same, ignoring the rising force.
questions.note: Spring work grows with x², not x.
questions.x: Spring energy grows with x², so later stretching costs more. The work from 0.1 m to 0.2 m is ½k(x₂² − x₁²) = 100 × 0.03 = 3 J, three times the 1 J needed for the first 0.1 m. Assuming equal steps cost equal work ignores that the force keeps rising.

questions.q: A 50 kg sledder starts from rest at the top of a 10 m high hill and reaches 10 m/s at the bottom. How much energy was lost to friction (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: mgh = 5000 J; KE = ½(50)(100) = 2500 J; lost 2500 J.
That is the total initial PE.
Adds KE to PE instead of subtracting.
0 J
The final KE is less than the initial PE, so energy was dissipated.
questions.x: Energy at the start is mgh = 50 × 10 × 10 = 5000 J. At the bottom, KE = ½ × 50 × 10² = 2500 J. The missing 2500 J was turned into heat by friction (W_friction = −2500 J). Energy lost is always the difference between the initial and final mechanical energy.

questions.q: Total mechanical energy of a system is conserved when:
o: The net force is zero
Net force can be nonzero (e.g., free fall) while energy is conserved.
Friction is present but small
Any friction dissipates some mechanical energy.
The object moves at constant speed
A block sliding at constant speed down a rough ramp loses mechanical energy.
Only conservative forces do work
Correct: nonconservative forces (friction, drag) convert mechanical energy to other forms.
questions.x: Mechanical energy (KE + PE) stays constant when only conservative forces, such as gravity and springs, do work. Friction, drag and muscles do nonconservative work and change it. A nonzero net force is fine: in free fall gravity is the net force, yet mechanical energy is conserved.

questions.q: In a lab, a solid ball rolling without slipping down a ramp consistently has about 30% less translational KE at the bottom than mgh predicts. What best explains this?
o: The ball's mass was too large
Mass cancels in comparing KE to mgh.
The local value of g is larger than assumed
A larger g would increase the KE.
Some energy goes into the ball's rotational kinetic energy
Correct: for a solid sphere, 2/7 of the energy (≈ 29%) is rotational.
The ramp height was underestimated
Underestimating h would make KE seem too large.
questions.x: A ball rolling without slipping has to spin as well as move forward. Part of mgh becomes rotational KE (½Iω²), so less is left for translational KE. For a solid sphere, I = ⅖mr², so 2/7 (≈29%) of the energy goes into rotation, which matches the data. Mass cancels, so mass cannot be the explanation.

questions.q: A 1 kg puck moving east at 3 m/s collides and sticks to a 1 kg puck moving north at 3 m/s. What is the velocity of the combined pucks?
o: 3 m/s toward the northeast
Adds the speeds then divides incorrectly.
About 2.1 m/s toward the northeast
Correct: p = (3, 3) kg·m/s; divided by 2 kg gives (1.5, 1.5), magnitude ≈ 2.1 m/s.
About 4.2 m/s toward the northeast
Forgets to divide by the combined mass.
0 m/s
Perpendicular momenta don't cancel.
questions.note: Conserve each momentum component separately.
questions.x: Conserve momentum separately in each direction: 3 kg·m/s east and 3 kg·m/s north. Dividing by the combined 2 kg gives 1.5 m/s in each direction, with magnitude 1.5√2 ≈ 2.1 m/s toward the northeast. Perpendicular momenta add as vectors, never cancel, and never add as plain numbers.

questions.q: Cart A (1 kg) moves at 4 m/s toward stationary cart B (1 kg). Afterward, A moves at 1 m/s and B at 3 m/s, both forward. How should this collision be classified?
o: Perfectly elastic
KE drops from 8 J to 5 J.
Perfectly inelastic
The carts move at different speeds, so they didn't stick.
Impossible, because momentum isn't conserved
1(1) + 1(3) = 4 kg·m/s, matching the initial momentum.
Inelastic, but not perfectly inelastic
Correct: momentum 4 → 4 is conserved, but KE falls from 8 J to 5 J and the carts separate.
questions.x: Check momentum first: 4 kg·m/s before, and 1 + 3 = 4 kg·m/s after, so it is conserved. KE drops from 8 J to 0.5 + 4.5 = 5 J, so the collision is not elastic. The carts separate, so it is not perfectly inelastic either. It falls in the general inelastic category.

questions.q: Two carts collide on a frictionless track with no external horizontal forces. What happens to the velocity of the system's center of mass?
o: It drops to zero at the moment of impact
Internal forces can't change the center of mass's motion.
It increases if the collision is elastic
Elasticity affects KE, not total momentum.
It remains constant
Correct: with no external force, total momentum and center-of-mass velocity don't change.
It reverses direction
That would require an external impulse.
questions.x: The center-of-mass velocity is the total momentum divided by the total mass. With no external force, the total momentum is constant, so the center-of-mass velocity stays the same no matter how violent or elastic the collision is. Internal forces redistribute momentum between the carts but cannot change the total.

questions.q: An ideal simple machine lets a person lift a load with a smaller effort force. Compared with lifting the load directly, which quantity is unchanged?
o: The effort force
It is smaller; reducing it is the purpose of the machine.
The work required
Correct: W = Fd; the smaller force acts over a proportionally longer distance.
The distance the effort must move
It is larger; a smaller force must act over a longer distance.
The ratio of load force to effort force
That ratio, the mechanical advantage, rises above 1.
questions.note: Machines trade force for distance, never saving work.
questions.x: An ideal machine cannot create energy, so the work needed to lift the load (mgh) is the same with or without it. It reduces the force by making the effort act over a proportionally longer distance, F_in d_in = F_out d_out. Real machines need slightly more input work because of friction.

questions.q: Lifting a box with a bent back, the erector spinae act about 5 cm behind the lumbar discs, while the upper body and box weight act about 40 cm in front. Why are disc forces so large?
o: The weight of the box acts directly on the discs only
Muscle force dominates the disc load.
Bending reduces the muscles' lever arm to zero
The lever arm is small but not zero.
Gravity is stronger when the back is bent
g is unchanged; lever arms change.
The short muscle lever arm requires a muscle force many times the load
Correct: about 8× the load (40/5), which adds compressive force on the discs.
questions.note: Bend the knees to bring the load closer.
questions.x: Taking torques about the disc, the back muscles' 5 cm lever arm must balance a load acting 40 cm in front. So the muscle force is about 8 times the load. The discs carry that muscle force plus the weight, which is why lifting with a bent back is dangerous. Keeping the load close shortens its lever arm.

questions.q: A saline solution has a density of 1200 kg/m³. What is its specific gravity?
o: Inverted ratio: water density divided by the solution density.
Correct: specific gravity = ρ/ρ(water) = 1200/1000, a dimensionless ratio.
This is the density itself; specific gravity divides by water's 1000 kg/m³.
1.2 kg/m³
Specific gravity is a ratio of densities, so it has no units.
questions.x: Specific gravity compares a substance's density with water's (1000 kg/m³ or 1 g/cm³), so the units cancel and only a pure number remains. Here 1200/1000 = 1.2, meaning the saline is 1.2 times as dense as water. A handy check: in g/cm³ the density and specific gravity are numerically equal, which is why attaching kg/m³ to 1.2 or reporting 1200 are both wrong.

questions.q: A patient's urine specific gravity rises from 1.005 to 1.030 after a day without drinking. This change indicates that the urine:
o: Contains more water per unit solute
That dilution would lower specific gravity toward 1.000.
Has a lower mass per unit volume
A higher specific gravity means a higher mass per unit volume.
Contains more dissolved solute per unit volume
Correct: added solute mass per volume raises density and thus specific gravity.
Has become less dense than water
Any specific gravity above 1 means denser than water.
questions.x: Urine specific gravity measures how much dissolved solute it carries per unit volume, since solutes add mass with little added volume. When the body conserves water, the kidneys excrete the same solutes in less water, so density and specific gravity rise toward 1.030. Values nearer 1.000 indicate dilute urine, so the rise means more solute per volume, not more water.

questions.q: Equal masses of two liquids with densities 800 kg/m³ and 1200 kg/m³ are mixed (volumes additive). The mixture's density is:
o: 960 kg/m³
1040 kg/m³
Weights toward the denser liquid; equal masses mean more volume of the lighter one.
2000 kg/m³
Densities are not additive; the sum of the two is meaningless.
1000 kg/m³
This simple average applies to equal volumes, not equal masses.
questions.x: For a mixture, density is total mass divided by total volume, not the average of the densities. With equal masses, the less dense liquid occupies more volume, so the mixture's density is pulled below the simple average of 1000 kg/m³ (it equals the harmonic mean, 2·800·1200/2000 = 960). A simple average is only correct when equal volumes are mixed.

questions.q: An open-ended mercury manometer is attached to a gas tank. The mercury on the open side stands 20 cm higher than on the tank side. The gauge pressure of the gas is about: (ρ(Hg) = 13,600 kg/m³)
o: That is the absolute pressure, not the gauge pressure.
A higher column on the open side means the gas pressure exceeds atmospheric.
Correct: the gas pushes mercury up the open arm; ρgh = 13,600 × 10 × 0.2 ≈ 2.7×10⁴ Pa above atmospheric.
Used the density of water instead of mercury.
questions.x: An open-tube manometer reads gauge pressure as the height difference between its two mercury surfaces: P(gas) − Patm = ρgh. If the open side is higher, the gas has pushed mercury toward the atmosphere, so the gas pressure exceeds atmospheric: 13,600 × 10 × 0.2 ≈ 2.7×10⁴ Pa. If the tank side were higher, the gauge pressure would be negative.

questions.q: An open beaker of water sits in an elevator accelerating upward at 2 m/s². What is the gauge pressure 1 m below the water surface?
o: That would be for downward acceleration (g − a).
This ignores the elevator's acceleration.
Correct: effective g = 10 + 2 = 12 m/s², so P = 1000 × 12 × 1 = 12,000 Pa.
Doubled g instead of adding the 2 m/s² acceleration to it.
questions.x: Hydrostatic pressure comes from supporting the fluid above a point, so it depends on the effective gravity in the fluid's frame. Accelerating upward at a requires each layer to push harder, giving g(eff) = g + a = 12 m/s² and P = ρ(g + a)h = 12,000 Pa. Downward acceleration would reduce it to g − a, and free fall would make the gauge pressure zero.

questions.q: In a hydraulic lift with an area ratio of 1:25, the small piston is pushed down 50 cm. How far does the large piston rise?
o: 10 cm
Used the radius ratio (5) instead of the area ratio.
Multiplied by 25; the large piston moves less, not more.
2 cm
Correct: equal volumes are displaced, so d₂ = 50 cm/25; work in equals work out.
50 cm
Equal distances would violate volume conservation.
questions.x: An incompressible fluid transfers volume: the volume pushed out by the small piston equals the volume that raises the large piston, so A₁d₁ = A₂d₂. With an area ratio of 1:25, the large piston moves 50 cm/25 = 2 cm. This matches energy conservation: the force is 25 times larger but the distance is 25 times smaller, so work in equals work out.

questions.q: Ignoring gravity, cerebrospinal fluid pressure at the skull rises by 20 mmHg. What change would a lumbar spinal needle in the same continuous fluid space register?
o: No change, because the needle is far from the skull
Distance does not diminish a transmitted pressure change.
An increase of 20 mmHg
Correct: by Pascal's principle the change is transmitted undiminished.
An increase much smaller than 20 mmHg
Pressure changes are not attenuated in an enclosed fluid.
An increase much larger than 20 mmHg
Pascal's principle transmits, not amplifies, pressure.
questions.x: Pascal's principle states that a pressure change in an enclosed, continuous fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout. Cerebrospinal fluid fills a connected space from skull to lumbar spine, so a 20 mmHg rise at the skull also appears at the lumbar needle. This is why lumbar puncture opening pressure can reflect intracranial pressure; distance does not attenuate the change.

questions.q: An object weighs 30 N in air and 20 N when fully submerged in water. What is its density?
o: 1500 kg/m³
Used 20 N rather than the 10 N buoyant force in the ratio.
2000 kg/m³
Divided the submerged weight by the buoyant force.
3000 kg/m³
Correct: F(b) = 10 N gives V = 10⁻³ m³; mass 3 kg / 10⁻³ m³ = 3000 kg/m³.
667 kg/m³
Inverted the ratio; an object that sinks must be denser than water.
questions.x: The loss of weight in water equals the buoyant force: 30 − 20 = 10 N, which corresponds to a displaced volume of 10/(1000 × 10) = 10⁻³ m³. The mass is 30/10 = 3 kg, so density = 3/10⁻³ = 3000 kg/m³. Equivalently, specific gravity = true weight/weight loss = 30/10 = 3. Using the 20 N apparent weight in place of the buoyant force is the main trap.

questions.q: An ice cube floats in a glass of fresh water filled to the brim. When the ice melts completely, the water level:
o: Rises, then falls back as it cools
No temperature effect is needed to reach the answer.
Stays the same
Correct: floating ice displaces its own weight of water, exactly the volume its meltwater fills.
Rises and overflows
The above-water portion is offset by ice being less dense than water.
Falls
Melted ice fills exactly the volume it was displacing.
questions.x: Floating ice displaces a mass of water equal to its own mass. When it melts, that same mass becomes liquid water that occupies exactly the volume the ice was displacing, so the level does not change. The portion of ice above the surface is compensated by ice being less dense than water, so the brimful glass does not overflow.

questions.q: A boat floating in a closed pool carries a large rock. The rock is dropped overboard and sinks. The pool's water level:
o: Falls
Correct: in the boat, the rock displaced its weight of water; sunk, it displaces only its smaller volume.
Rises
A sunken dense rock displaces less water than when floating in the boat.
Rises, then returns to the original level
The final level is lower, not unchanged.
Stays the same
This would be true only if the rock had the density of water.
questions.x: A floating object displaces its weight of water, while a sunken object displaces only its own volume. In the boat, the dense rock displaced water equal to its weight, which is more than its volume of water. Once it sinks, it displaces only its volume, so the total displaced water decreases and the pool level falls.

questions.q: A 0.001 m³ block of wood (density 600 kg/m³) is held fully under water by a string tied to the bottom of the tank. What is the tension in the string?
o: 4 N
Correct: buoyant force 10 N minus weight 6 N leaves 4 N of tension.
Added the weight to the buoyant force; they act in opposite directions.
That is the buoyant force alone.
6 N
That is the block's weight, not the string tension.
questions.x: For an object held underwater, the forces balance: buoyant force (up) = weight (down) + string tension (down). Buoyant force = 1000 × 0.001 × 10 = 10 N, and weight = 600 × 0.001 × 10 = 6 N, so T = 10 − 6 = 4 N. The string pulls down because the wood would float if released; adding the forces instead treats them as acting in the same direction.

questions.q: Blood leaves the aorta (area 4 cm²) at 25 cm/s. The total cross-sectional area of all systemic capillaries is about 2500 cm². What is the average speed of blood in the capillaries?
o: 625 cm/s
Multiplied by the area ratio instead of dividing.
25 cm/s
Speed must fall when total area increases.
Correct: Q = 100 cm³/s; v = 100/2500 = 0.04 cm/s.
0.4 cm/s
Off by a factor of 10 in the division.
questions.x: By continuity, flow rate is conserved across the whole circulation, so v depends on the total cross-sectional area of each vessel level. Aortic flow Q = 4 × 25 = 100 cm³/s; spread over 2500 cm² of capillaries, v = 0.04 cm/s. Even though each capillary is tiny, their combined area is huge, so blood moves slowest there, allowing time for exchange.

questions.q: An artery divides into 4 identical branches, each with half the parent's radius. Compared with the parent, the average flow speed in each branch is:
o: Four times larger
Considered one branch's area only, ignoring that flow is shared.
Twice as large
Used radius rather than area in the calculation.
Half as large
Doubled the total area by mistake.
The same
Correct: total branch area = 4 × (1/2)² = 1 times the parent area.
questions.x: Continuity applies to the total area of parallel branches, not the area of a single branch. Each branch has (1/2)² = 1/4 the parent's area, and four of them together equal the parent's area, so the average speed is unchanged. Considering one branch alone, or using radius instead of area, gives a false speed change.

questions.q: During a storm, strong wind blowing horizontally across a flat roof lifts the roof off a house. This is best explained by:
o: Lower pressure in the fast-moving air above the roof
Correct: by Bernoulli's principle, faster air over the roof has lower pressure than the still air inside.
Buoyancy of the roof in the surrounding air
The roof's buoyant force is tiny and does not change with wind speed.
Wind pushing directly upward on the roof surface
A horizontal wind exerts no direct upward push on a flat roof.
Higher pressure in the fast-moving air above the roof
Faster-moving air has lower static pressure, not higher.
questions.note: Faster flow means lower static pressure.
questions.x: Bernoulli's principle links fast-moving air with lower static pressure. Wind racing over a roof lowers the pressure above it, while the still air inside the building stays near atmospheric, so a net upward force acts on the roof. A horizontal wind cannot directly push a roof upward, and buoyancy is unchanged by wind and far too small to lift it.

questions.q: Which is an assumption of Poiseuille's law?
o: Turbulent flow through a flexible tube
Turbulence and wall flexibility violate the law's assumptions.
Flow of a fluid with zero viscosity
Poiseuille's law is built on viscosity; η is in the formula.
Compressible gas flow at high speed
The law assumes incompressible, slow, laminar flow.
Laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a rigid cylindrical tube
Correct: the law requires steady laminar flow with constant viscosity.
questions.x: Poiseuille's law is derived for steady, laminar flow of an incompressible Newtonian fluid (constant viscosity) through a long, rigid, cylindrical tube. Turbulence, flexible walls, compressibility or a non-Newtonian fluid all break those assumptions. It also requires viscosity, since the law describes flow resisted by viscous friction; a zero-viscosity fluid has no Poiseuille resistance.

questions.q: Two vessel segments of equal length are in series; the second has half the radius of the first. Approximately what fraction of the total pressure drop occurs across the narrow segment?
o: Equal drops would require equal resistances.
Treated resistance as scaling with 1/r.
Treated resistance as scaling with 1/r².
Correct: R₂ = 16R₁, so the narrow segment takes 16/17 ≈ 94% of ΔP.
questions.x: In series, the same flow passes through both segments, so each segment's pressure drop is proportional to its resistance (ΔP = QR). Halving the radius raises resistance by 2⁴ = 16, so the drops are in the ratio 1:16, and the narrow segment takes 16/17 ≈ 94%. This is why most pressure loss occurs at the narrowest points, such as arterioles.

questions.q: Unlike liquids, the viscosity of a gas increases with temperature. The best explanation is that, at higher temperature, gas molecules:
o: Become more densely packed
At constant pressure, heating lowers gas density.
Form temporary hydrogen-bonded clusters
Heating breaks, rather than forms, such clusters.
Move faster and transfer more momentum between layers
Correct: gas viscosity comes from momentum exchange, which rises with speed.
Attract each other more strongly
Intermolecular attractions are weak and do not grow with temperature.
questions.x: In a gas, molecules are far apart and attractions are negligible; viscosity arises because molecules moving between layers carry momentum and drag neighboring layers along. Heating speeds up the molecules and increases this momentum transfer, so gas viscosity rises. In liquids, heating disrupts intermolecular attractions and lowers viscosity, the opposite trend.

questions.q: While a blood pressure cuff is deflated between systolic and diastolic pressure, Korotkoff sounds are heard. These sounds arise because flow through the partly compressed artery is:
o: Turbulent
Correct: high-speed flow through the narrowed artery becomes turbulent and noisy.
Flowing backward
Flow in the artery remains forward.
Completely stopped
With no flow there is no sound; that occurs above systolic pressure.
Laminar
Laminar flow is silent; it returns once cuff pressure falls below diastolic and the sounds stop.
questions.x: Between systolic and diastolic pressure, the cuff partly compresses the artery, so blood spurts through a narrowed opening at high speed. This raises the Reynolds number enough for turbulence, which produces audible Korotkoff sounds. Above systolic no blood flows, and below diastolic the artery stays open with quiet laminar flow, so sounds start and stop at those pressures.

questions.q: Blood is a shear-thinning (non-Newtonian) fluid. As the shear rate increases, for example during fast flow, blood's apparent viscosity:
o: Increases, as red cells collide more often
That would describe a shear-thickening fluid.
Decreases, as red cells disaggregate and align with flow
Correct: shear-thinning fluids become less viscous at higher shear.
Is unchanged, as with water
Water is Newtonian; blood is not.
Drops to zero
Viscosity falls but never reaches zero.
questions.x: Blood's apparent viscosity depends on shear rate, making it non-Newtonian. At low shear, red cells aggregate into stacks (rouleaux) that resist flow; at high shear these break up and the cells deform and align with the flow, so viscosity falls (shear thinning). A shear-thickening fluid does the opposite, and a Newtonian fluid such as water has constant viscosity.

questions.q: At very high pressure, a real gas often occupies a larger volume than the ideal gas law predicts. The main reason is that:
o: Gas molecules have a finite volume of their own
Correct: excluded molecular volume becomes significant when gas is compressed.
Collisions with the walls become elastic
Ideal gases already assume elastic collisions.
Intermolecular attractions pull molecules together
Attractions make the volume smaller, not larger.
Molecules move faster at high pressure
Speed depends on temperature, not pressure.
questions.x: Real molecules take up space, so the volume actually available for motion is less than the container volume. At very high pressure the molecules are packed closely and this excluded volume becomes significant, making the real volume larger than PV = nRT predicts (the b term in van der Waals). Attractions push the other way, making volume smaller, and dominate at moderate pressures and low temperatures.

questions.q: A diver fills her lungs to 2 L at 20 m depth (about 3 atm absolute), then holds her breath and ascends to the surface. Her lung gas would expand to about:
o: 4 L
Used gauge pressure (2 atm) instead of absolute pressure.
2 L
Gas volume changes with pressure.
6 L
Correct: Boyle's law, 3 atm × 2 L = 1 atm × V, so V = 6 L, risking barotrauma.
Gas expands, not compresses, as pressure falls.
questions.x: Boyle's law uses absolute pressure: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. At 20 m the absolute pressure is about 3 atm, and at the surface 1 atm, so 3 × 2 L = 1 × V gives V = 6 L, enough to overexpand and rupture lungs. This is why divers must exhale while ascending. Using gauge pressure (2 atm) underestimates the expansion.

questions.q: Air (21% O₂) is inhaled at sea level (760 mmHg) and fully humidified at body temperature, where water vapor pressure is 47 mmHg. The PO₂ of the humidified air is about:
o: 100 mmHg
That is alveolar PO₂, which also reflects CO₂ and O₂ uptake.
160 mmHg
Ignores water vapor; 0.21 × 760 ≈ 160 mmHg.
150 mmHg
113 mmHg
Took 21% of 760 and then subtracted all 47 mmHg of vapor from the O₂ alone.
questions.x: In the airways, inspired air becomes saturated with water vapor at body temperature, and water vapor takes up 47 mmHg of the total pressure. The remaining dry-gas pressure is 760 − 47 = 713 mmHg, and O₂ is 21% of that: ≈150 mmHg. Alveolar PO₂ is lower still (~100 mmHg) because O₂ is taken up and CO₂ is added.

questions.q: Helium is pumped into a rigid, sealed container of air at constant temperature, doubling the total pressure. The partial pressure of O₂ in the container:
o: Halves
O₂'s mole fraction halves, but total pressure doubles, so P(O₂) is constant.
Falls to zero
Helium does not remove O₂.
Doubles
Only total pressure doubles; O₂ amount did not change.
Is unchanged
Correct: O₂ moles, volume and T are unchanged, so its partial pressure is too.
questions.x: Each gas's partial pressure depends only on its own moles, the volume and the temperature (P = nRT/V), as if it filled the container alone. Adding helium to a rigid container raises the total pressure but leaves O₂'s moles, the volume and the temperature unchanged, so P(O₂) is constant. O₂'s mole fraction halves, but the total pressure doubles, and the two effects cancel.

questions.q: Across the alveolar membrane, the PO₂ gradient is about 60 mmHg while the PCO₂ gradient is only about 6 mmHg, yet CO₂ exchange is not limited. The best explanation is that CO₂:
o: Is far more soluble in water and tissue than O₂
Correct: CO₂'s solubility is about 20 times O₂'s, offsetting its small gradient.
Is actively transported across the membrane
Gas exchange is passive diffusion.
Has a lower molar mass than O₂
CO₂ (44 g/mol) is heavier than O₂ (32 g/mol).
Has a higher partial pressure in air than O₂
Atmospheric PCO₂ is far below PO₂.
questions.x: Diffusion rate across a membrane depends on the partial pressure gradient times the gas's solubility (Fick's law), among other factors. CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble than O₂ in water and tissue, so a small PCO₂ gradient moves as much CO₂ as a large PO₂ gradient moves O₂. CO₂ is actually heavier than O₂, so molar mass does not explain its fast exchange.

questions.q: Raising a patient's PaO₂ from 100 to 600 mmHg increases arterial O₂ content only modestly. Why?
o: Extra O₂ lowers plasma solubility
Solubility is a constant at a given temperature.
Henry's law stops applying above 100 mmHg
Dissolved O₂ keeps rising linearly with PO₂.
Hemoglobin is already nearly saturated, and dissolved O₂ rises only by a small amount
Correct: dissolved O₂ climbs linearly but stays small relative to Hb-bound O₂.
High PO₂ causes hemoglobin to release O₂
Higher PO₂ favors O₂ binding, not release.
questions.x: Arterial O₂ content is mostly hemoglobin-bound O₂, plus a small dissolved fraction (0.003 mL/dL per mmHg). At PaO₂ 100 mmHg hemoglobin is already about 98% saturated, so raising PaO₂ to 600 mmHg adds little bound O₂ and only about 1.5 mL/dL dissolved O₂. Henry's law still applies linearly; the dissolved amount is simply small.

questions.q: Plasma equilibrates with alveolar gas at PO₂ = 100 mmHg and PCO₂ = 40 mmHg. Comparing dissolved gases, the plasma contains:
o: More dissolved CO₂ than O₂, despite CO₂'s lower partial pressure
Correct: CO₂'s ~20× higher solubility outweighs its lower partial pressure.
Equal concentrations of both gases
Equal concentrations would require equal solubility × pressure.
No dissolved CO₂, since it is all converted to bicarbonate
Some CO₂ always remains physically dissolved.
More dissolved O₂ than CO₂, because PO₂ is higher
Concentration depends on solubility as well as partial pressure.
questions.x: Dissolved gas concentration equals solubility times partial pressure (Henry's law). CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble than O₂, so even at 40 mmHg its dissolved concentration (∝ 20 × 40 = 800) exceeds that of O₂ at 100 mmHg (∝ 1 × 100). Partial pressure alone does not determine how much gas dissolves.

questions.q: An experimenter measures flow through a rigid tube at several pressure differences. Flow doubles when ΔP doubles at low ΔP, but at high ΔP, doubling ΔP raises flow by only about 40%. The best interpretation is that:
o: The fluid's viscosity fell at high ΔP
Lower viscosity would increase, not reduce, the flow gain.
The tube's radius increased at high ΔP
The tube is rigid; a wider tube would raise flow.
Poiseuille's law holds at all pressures
Poiseuille predicts doubling, which was not observed.
Flow became turbulent at high ΔP
Correct: turbulent flow scales roughly with √ΔP (√2 ≈ 1.4).
questions.x: Poiseuille's law predicts flow proportional to ΔP for laminar flow, matching the low-pressure data. At high ΔP, flow rose only about 40% (√2 ≈ 1.4) when ΔP doubled, which is the signature of turbulence, where energy is lost to eddies and Q ∝ √ΔP. A rigid tube rules out widening, and lower viscosity would increase rather than decrease the flow gain.

questions.q: A positively charged rod is held near a neutral metal sphere. The sphere is briefly grounded, the ground is removed, and then the rod is taken away. What is the sphere's final charge?
o: Negative
Correct: the rod draws electrons up from ground; they are trapped when ground is cut.
Positive
Induction gives a charge opposite to the inducing rod.
Neutral
Grounding while the rod is near lets net charge flow in.
Positive near the rod, net neutral
That is polarization without grounding; grounding adds net charge.
questions.note: Charging by induction leaves the opposite sign of the inducing charge.
questions.x: The positive rod attracts electrons toward the sphere; grounding provides a path for electrons from the earth to flow onto it. Breaking the ground connection first traps those extra electrons, so removing the rod leaves the sphere net negative. Without grounding, the sphere would only polarize and remain neutral overall.

questions.q: A charge +q sits at x = 0 and a charge +4q sits at x = 3 m. At what position would a small test charge feel zero net electrostatic force?
o: The midpoint balances only equal charges.
x = 2 m
Places the point closer to the larger charge; it must be closer to the smaller one.
x = 1 m
Correct: q/x² = 4q/(3 − x)² gives 3 − x = 2x, so x = 1 m.
x = −1 m, left of +q
Outside the pair, both repulsive forces point the same way and cannot cancel.
questions.x: The null point for two like charges lies between them, closer to the smaller charge, where the two repulsive forces point in opposite directions. Setting kq/x² = k(4q)/(3 − x)² and taking square roots gives 3 − x = 2x, so x = 1 m. The midpoint only works for equal charges, and points outside the pair cannot balance because both forces point the same way there.

questions.q: The ratio of electric force to gravitational force between two protons is about 10³⁶. How does this ratio change if the protons are moved twice as far apart?
o: It decreases by a factor of 4
Both forces drop by 4, so the ratio does not change.
It increases by a factor of 4
Neither force weakens more slowly than the other.
It decreases by a factor of 2
Neither force goes as 1/r, and they share the same r-dependence.
It stays the same
Correct: both forces scale as 1/r², so their ratio is independent of distance.
questions.x: Coulomb's law (kq²/r²) and Newton's gravitation (Gm²/r²) both fall off as 1/r². Doubling r cuts each force by the same factor of 4, so their ratio is unchanged at any separation. The ratio depends only on the particles' charges and masses, which is why gravity is negligible at atomic scales.

questions.q: Charges +q and −q are a distance d apart. What is the electric field at the midpoint?
o: Zero
Fields of opposite charges add at the midpoint; potential is zero there.
4kq/d², pointing toward +q
Fields point away from + and toward −, and both contributions add.
8kq/d², pointing toward −q
Correct: each gives kq/(d/2)² = 4kq/d², both pointing toward −q.
2kq/d², pointing toward −q
Uses d instead of d/2 for each distance.
questions.note: Trap: V = 0 at a dipole's midpoint, but E is not.
questions.x: At a dipole's midpoint the field from +q points away from +q, and the field from −q points toward −q: both point toward −q, so they add. Each has magnitude kq/(d/2)² = 4kq/d², giving 8kq/d². The trap is answering zero: the scalar potential cancels there, but the field vectors do not.

questions.q: A proton and an electron are released from rest in the same uniform electric field. Which statement is true?
o: The proton feels a larger force because it is heavier
F = qE depends on charge, not mass.
The forces have equal magnitude, but the electron accelerates far more
Correct: |q| is equal, and a = qE/m is larger for the much lighter electron.
Both have the same acceleration in opposite directions
Equal forces on unequal masses give unequal accelerations.
The electron feels a larger force because it is smaller
Size does not enter F = qE; charges have equal magnitude.
questions.x: The force in a field is F = qE, and the proton and electron have charges of equal magnitude, so the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction. Acceleration is a = F/m, and the electron is about 1800 times lighter, so it accelerates about 1800 times more. Mass affects acceleration, not the electric force itself.

questions.q: A hollow metal box is placed in a strong external electric field. Once charges settle, what is the field inside the box's empty interior?
o: Equal to the external field
Conductors shield their interiors; the field does not pass through unchanged.
Twice the external field
Induced charges cancel the field inside rather than reinforce it.
Equal and opposite to the external field
The net interior field is zero, not reversed.
Zero
Correct: surface charges rearrange until they cancel the field inside a conductor.
questions.note: This is the Faraday cage effect.
questions.x: Free charges in a conductor shift in an external field until the field they create exactly cancels the external field inside the metal. For a closed conducting shell with no charge inside the cavity, the cavity field is also zero, which is why a Faraday cage shields its contents. The field is cancelled, not reversed or reflected.

questions.q: An oil drop of mass 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg hangs motionless in an upward electric field of 1 × 10⁵ N/C. What is its charge? (g = 10 m/s²)
o: −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (one extra electron)
A negative charge would be pushed down, opposite the upward field.
+3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (two electrons missing)
Doubles the weight; mg is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N.
+1.6 × 10⁻²⁰ C (one-tenth of e)
Power-of-ten slip; the result is exactly one elementary charge.
+1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (one electron missing)
Correct: qE = mg gives q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴/10⁵; upward force with upward E means positive.
questions.x: For the drop to hang still, the electric force must balance gravity: qE = mg. Here mg = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵)(10) = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, so |q| = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 10⁵ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The electric force must point up, the same direction as E, so the charge is positive (one electron missing).

questions.q: In a mass spectrometer, two ions with equal charge and equal speed enter the same magnetic field. Ion 2 has twice the mass of ion 1. Compared with ion 1, ion 2's path radius is:
o: Twice as large
Correct: r = mv/(qB) is proportional to m at fixed q, v and B.
Half as large
Heavier ions are harder to deflect, so they curve less.
Four times as large
r scales linearly with m, not with m².
The same
Mass does affect the radius.
questions.x: Setting the magnetic force equal to the centripetal force gives r = mv/(qB). With equal q, v and B, the radius is directly proportional to mass, so doubling m doubles r. Heavier ions have more momentum and curve less sharply, which is how a mass spectrometer separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio.

questions.q: Which 0.1 M aqueous solution conducts electricity best?
o: NaCl
Gives only 2 ions per formula unit.
Acetic acid
A weak acid; only a small fraction ionizes.
CaCl₂
Correct: it dissociates into 3 ions per formula unit, the most charge carriers here.
Glucose
A nonelectrolyte; it forms no ions.
questions.note: Solution conductivity tracks the concentration of mobile ions.
questions.x: Solution conductivity depends on the concentration and charge of mobile ions. At equal molarity, CaCl₂ fully dissociates into three ions (Ca²⁺ and 2 Cl⁻), carrying more total charge than NaCl's two ions. Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte that barely ionizes, and glucose produces no ions at all.

questions.q: Wires A and B are made of the same metal and carry the same current, but B has half the cross-sectional area of A. How does the electron drift speed in B compare with A?
o: Half as fast
Inverts the relationship; a narrower wire needs faster drift.
Twice as fast
Correct: I = nqAv_d, so halving A at fixed I and n doubles v_d.
Four times as fast
v_d is inversely proportional to A, not to A².
The same
Same current through a smaller area requires a higher drift speed.
questions.x: Current relates to carrier motion by I = nqAv_d, where n is the carrier density and v_d the drift speed. With the same metal (same n) and same current, v_d is inversely proportional to A, so halving the area doubles the drift speed. The same charge per second must squeeze through a smaller cross-section.

questions.q: A 24 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 12 Ω resistors. What is the current through the 12 Ω resistor?
o: 3 A
That is the total current, which splits between the branches.
2 A
That is the current through the 6 Ω branch.
Splits the 3 A equally; parallel branches share voltage, not current.
1 A
Correct: the pair is 4 Ω, total 8 Ω, I = 3 A; the pair has 12 V, so 12/12 = 1 A.
questions.x: First reduce the parallel pair: 6 × 12/(6 + 12) = 4 Ω, so the total is 8 Ω and the battery supplies 24/8 = 3 A. The 4 Ω series resistor drops 12 V, leaving 12 V across the pair, so the 12 Ω branch carries 12/12 = 1 A and the 6 Ω branch 2 A. Current splits inversely to resistance, not equally.

questions.q: A battery with an emf of 9 V and an internal resistance of 1 Ω is connected to a 2 Ω external resistor. What is the terminal voltage?
o: 9 V
Terminal voltage equals emf only when no current flows.
6 V
3 V
That is the drop across the internal resistance.
Uses I = 9/2 and ignores the internal resistance in the current.
questions.note: V_terminal = emf − Ir.
questions.x: A real battery has internal resistance r, so the current is I = emf/(R + r) = 9/3 = 3 A. Part of the emf is lost inside the battery, Ir = 3 V, so the terminal voltage is 9 − 3 = 6 V, which is also IR across the 2 Ω load. The terminal voltage equals the emf only when no current flows.

questions.q: A 2 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor are wired in parallel across a battery. How does the power dissipated by the 2 Ω resistor compare with the 8 Ω resistor?
o: One-fourth as much
That is the series result, where P = I²R.
The same
Equal voltage does not mean equal power when R differs.
Twice as much
The ratio of resistances is 4, so P differs by 4.
4 times as much
Correct: same V in parallel, and P = V²/R is larger for the smaller R.
questions.note: Parallel: smaller R gets more power. Series: larger R gets more power.
questions.x: Parallel resistors share the same voltage, so the useful power formula is P = V²/R, which is inversely proportional to R. The 2 Ω resistor dissipates 8/2 = 4 times as much power as the 8 Ω resistor. In series the opposite holds: same current, P = I²R, so the larger resistor gets more power.

questions.q: A power line delivers the same power to a town, but the transmission voltage is doubled. How does the power lost as heat in the line change?
o: It halves
Loss depends on I², not I.
It quadruples
Uses V²/R with the full line voltage, which is not the drop across the line.
It falls to one-fourth
Correct: I halves at fixed P = IV, and loss I²R falls 4×.
It does not change
Lower current reduces resistive loss.
questions.note: High-voltage transmission cuts current and I²R losses.
questions.x: To deliver a fixed power P = IV, doubling the transmission voltage halves the current. Heat lost in the line is I²R_line, so halving I cuts the loss to one quarter. Using V²/R with the transmission voltage is the trap; the voltage drop across the line itself is IR_line, which also falls.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor stays connected to a battery while its plates are pulled to twice their separation. What happens to the stored charge?
o: It halves
Correct: V is fixed by the battery and C halves, so Q = CV halves.
It stays the same
Charge is fixed only if the capacitor is isolated.
It doubles
Increasing d decreases C, so Q falls.
It quarters
C goes as 1/d, so Q falls by 2, not 4.
questions.note: Connected to a battery: V constant. Isolated: Q constant.
questions.x: While a capacitor stays connected to a battery, its voltage is fixed by the battery. Doubling the plate separation halves C = ε₀A/d, so Q = CV must also halve, with charge flowing back into the battery. Charge stays constant only if the capacitor is isolated from the battery.

questions.q: A charged parallel-plate capacitor is disconnected from its battery, and then its plate separation is doubled. What happens to the stored energy?
o: It halves
That would be true at constant voltage, not constant charge.
It stays the same
Work is done pulling the attracting plates apart, so U rises.
It doubles
Correct: Q is fixed, C halves, so U = Q²/(2C) doubles.
It quadruples
U goes as 1/C, and C only halves.
questions.x: Disconnected from the battery, the capacitor's charge Q stays fixed. Doubling d halves C, and with U = Q²/(2C), the energy doubles. The extra energy comes from the work done pulling the oppositely charged plates apart against their attraction; 'halves' would apply at constant voltage instead.

questions.q: A dielectric of constant κ is slid between the plates of a charged capacitor that has been disconnected from its battery. What happens to the stored energy?
o: It increases by a factor of κ
That occurs if the battery stays connected (V fixed).
It stays the same
C changes while Q is fixed, so U changes.
It increases by a factor of κ squared
U depends on 1/C, which changes only by κ.
It decreases by a factor of κ
Correct: Q is fixed and C rises κ-fold, so U = Q²/(2C) falls by κ.
questions.x: An isolated capacitor keeps a fixed charge Q. Inserting a dielectric multiplies C by κ, and since U = Q²/(2C), the stored energy falls by a factor of κ. The field does work pulling the dielectric in, which accounts for the lost energy. With a battery connected (V fixed), U = ½CV² would rise by κ instead.

questions.q: How does inserting a dielectric between a capacitor's plates allow it to store more charge at a given voltage?
o: It conducts charge between the plates
A conductor would short the capacitor; dielectrics insulate.
Its molecules polarize, creating a field that partly cancels the plates' field
Correct: the reduced net field lowers V for a given Q, so C rises.
It adds free electrons to the negative plate
Dielectrics do not supply free charge.
It increases the area of the plates
Plate area is unchanged; the dielectric acts through polarization.
questions.x: A dielectric's molecules polarize in the field, with their charges lining up to create an internal field opposite the plates' field. This reduces the net field and therefore the voltage for a given charge, so C = Q/V rises by a factor of κ. A dielectric is an insulator; it does not conduct or add free charge.

questions.q: What is the sign of the anode in an electrolytic cell?
o: Negative
The anode is negative in a galvanic cell, not an electrolytic one.
Neutral
The external source gives each electrode a sign.
Positive
Correct: the external source pulls electrons out of the anode, making it positive.
Positive or negative, depending on the metal
In electrolytic cells the anode is always positive.
questions.note: Anode sign: galvanic −, electrolytic +.
questions.x: In an electrolytic cell, an external power source drives a nonspontaneous reaction by pulling electrons out of the anode and pushing them into the cathode. That makes the anode positive and the cathode negative. Oxidation still occurs at the anode; only the sign is reversed relative to a galvanic cell, where the anode is negative.

questions.q: In a galvanic cell's salt bridge, which way do anions migrate?
o: Toward the cathode compartment
Cations move toward the cathode; anions go the other way.
Toward the anode compartment
Correct: anions balance the positive charge building up as metal cations form at the anode.
They do not move; only cations migrate
Both ions in the bridge migrate to keep neutrality.
Into the external wire
Ions cannot travel through the metal wire.
questions.x: As a galvanic cell runs, the anode compartment gains cations (metal is oxidized to ions) and the cathode compartment loses cations (ions are reduced to metal). To keep each solution electrically neutral, anions from the salt bridge migrate toward the anode and cations toward the cathode. Ions never travel through the external wire; only electrons do.

questions.q: A concentrated aqueous NaCl solution is electrolyzed. What forms at the cathode?
o: Hydrogen gas
Correct: water is far easier to reduce than Na⁺, so H₂ evolves.
Sodium metal
Na⁺ has a very negative reduction potential; water is reduced first.
Chlorine gas
Chlorine forms by oxidation at the anode.
Oxygen gas
Oxygen would come from oxidation at the anode.
questions.note: In water, highly active metal ions are not reduced; water is.
questions.x: In aqueous solution, the cathode reduces whichever species is easiest to reduce. Na⁺ has a very negative reduction potential (−2.71 V), so water is reduced instead, producing H₂ gas and OH⁻. This differs from molten NaCl, where no water is present and sodium metal forms.

questions.q: In a galvanic cell's salt bridge containing KNO₃, which way do K⁺ ions move?
o: Toward the cathode compartment
Correct: they replace positive charge lost as cations are reduced at the cathode.
Toward the anode compartment
That is the direction of NO₃⁻.
Through the wire to the anode
Ions do not travel through the metal wire.
They stay put while only NO₃⁻ moves
Both ions migrate to keep both solutions neutral.
questions.x: In the cathode compartment, cations such as Cu²⁺ are removed as they are reduced, leaving excess negative charge. K⁺ ions from the salt bridge migrate into the cathode compartment to restore neutrality, while NO₃⁻ ions move toward the anode compartment, where cations are being produced. Ions never travel through the wire.

questions.q: Al³⁺/Al has E°red = −1.66 V and Ni²⁺/Ni has E°red = −0.25 V. What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from them?
o: Adds the magnitudes instead of taking the difference.
Divides by 3 for the three electrons; E° is intensive.
Doubles the potential for stoichiometry; E° is intensive.
Correct: E°cathode − E°anode = −0.25 − (−1.66).
questions.x: The cathode is the half-reaction with the higher E°red: Ni²⁺/Ni at −0.25 V; aluminum, at −1.66 V, is oxidized at the anode. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = −0.25 − (−1.66) = +1.41 V. Electron counts (3 for Al, 2 for Ni) affect balancing, never E°, because potential is intensive.

questions.q: A student pairs an unknown metal M with a standard hydrogen electrode. M acts as the anode, and the cell reads +0.44 V. What is E°red for M²⁺/M?
o: +0.44 V (above hydrogen)
If M were reduced more easily than H⁺, it would be the cathode.
Divides by n; potentials do not scale with electrons.
−0.44 V (below hydrogen)
Correct: E°cell = 0 − E°(M) = +0.44, so E°(M) = −0.44 V.
Doubles for 2 electrons; E° is intensive.
questions.x: When M is the anode, it is oxidized and the SHE (E° = 0) is the cathode. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode gives 0.44 = 0 − E°(M), so E°(M) = −0.44 V. A metal that acts as an anode against SHE must lie below hydrogen in reduction potential, so a positive value is impossible.

questions.q: Two hydrogen electrodes (1 atm H₂) are in solutions at pH 1 and pH 4. What is the voltage of this concentration cell at 25 °C? (Use 0.06/n per decade.)
o: About 0.09 V
Applies n = 2 without squaring [H⁺] in Q.
About 0.18 V
Correct: [H⁺] differs by 10³; 0.06 V per decade for H⁺ gives 0.06 × 3.
About 0.30 V
Adds the pH values (1 + 4 = 5 decades) instead of taking their difference.
0 V
That is E°; unequal [H⁺] produces a voltage.
questions.x: The half-reaction 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ has n = 2, but Q contains [H⁺]², so E = (0.06/2) log([H⁺]conc/[H⁺]dil)² = 0.06 log(ratio). pH 1 versus pH 4 is a 10³ ratio, giving 0.06 × 3 = 0.18 V. Using n = 2 without squaring the concentrations gives the 0.09 V trap.

questions.q: Two identical 1.5 V cells are connected in parallel to a load. Compared with one cell, what does this arrangement provide?
o: 3.0 V with the same run time
That describes cells in series.
0.75 V with a longer run time
Parallel identical sources do not divide the voltage.
The same 1.5 V but a longer run time
Correct: parallel cells share the current, keeping 1.5 V while doubling capacity.
3.0 V with a longer run time
Parallel connection does not add voltage.
questions.x: Identical cells in parallel share the same two terminals, so the output voltage stays at 1.5 V. The load current is split between them, so each cell supplies half as much, and the pair lasts about twice as long. Connecting the cells in series would add voltages to 3.0 V without increasing capacity.

questions.q: How does a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell differ from an ordinary battery?
o: It oxidizes O₂ at the anode
O₂ is reduced at the cathode; H₂ is oxidized at the anode.
It needs an external power source to run
A fuel cell is galvanic; its reaction is spontaneous.
Its reactants are supplied continuously from outside
Correct: H₂ and O₂ are fed in, so it runs as long as fuel flows.
Its electrons flow from cathode to anode
As in all galvanic cells, electrons flow from anode to cathode.
questions.x: A fuel cell is a galvanic cell whose reactants, H₂ and O₂, are supplied continuously from outside rather than sealed inside. H₂ is oxidized at the anode and O₂ reduced at the cathode, with electrons flowing from anode to cathode as in any galvanic cell. It runs as long as fuel is supplied.

questions.q: A species contains 26 protons, 30 neutrons and 23 electrons. Which symbol represents it?
o: ⁵⁶Fe³⁻
Fewer electrons than protons gives a positive charge, not a negative one.
⁵⁶Mn³⁺
Element identity is set by the 26 protons, which makes it iron, not manganese.
⁴⁹Fe³⁺
Mass number counts protons plus neutrons (56), not protons plus electrons.
⁵⁶Fe³⁺
Correct: Z = 26 is Fe, A = 26 + 30 = 56, and charge = 26 − 23 = +3.
questions.x: Read a species in three steps: protons give the element (26 = Fe), protons plus neutrons give the mass number (56), and protons minus electrons give the charge (+3). Having fewer electrons than protons always makes a cation. Changing electrons never changes the element, which rules out manganese.

questions.q: Boron has an average atomic mass of 10.8 u and consists of ¹⁰B and ¹¹B. What is the approximate percent abundance of ¹¹B?
o: That is the abundance of ¹⁰B, not ¹¹B.
A 50:50 mix would average 10.5 u.
Correct: 10x + 11(1 − x) = 10.8 gives x = 0.2 for ¹⁰B, so ¹¹B is 80%.
Too high; that would give an average near 10.92 u.
questions.x: Set up a weighted average with one unknown: if x is the fraction of ¹⁰B, then 10x + 11(1 − x) = 10.8, so x = 0.2 and ¹¹B is 80%. A quick check: 10.8 lies 80% of the way from 10 to 11, so the heavier isotope dominates. The 20% choice is the lighter isotope's abundance, a common mix-up.

questions.q: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through while a few bounced back. What did this show?
o: Electrons occupy quantized orbits
Quantized orbits came from Bohr's model and line spectra, not this experiment.
Positive charge is spread evenly through the atom
That plum-pudding picture predicted no large-angle deflections.
The nucleus contains neutral neutrons
Neutrons were discovered later by Chadwick.
Mass and positive charge sit in a tiny dense nucleus
Correct: mostly empty space explains pass-through; a dense core explains rare rebounds.
questions.x: Most alpha particles passing straight through means the atom is mostly empty space; the rare large-angle rebounds mean positive charge and nearly all mass are packed into a tiny, dense nucleus. The plum-pudding model, with positive charge spread evenly, predicted only small deflections. Quantized orbits came later from Bohr's work on hydrogen spectra.

questions.q: Bromine is about 50% ⁷⁹Br and 50% ⁸¹Br. In a mass spectrum of Br₂, what intensity ratio is expected for peaks at m/z 158, 160 and 162?
o: Ignores that ⁷⁹Br⁸¹Br can form two ways (79–81 and 81–79).
Correct: probabilities are ¼ (79,79), ½ (79,81 either order), ¼ (81,81).
Overcounts the mixed combination.
Inverts the result; the mixed pair is the most likely.
questions.x: Treat each Br atom as an independent 50:50 choice. The combinations are 79–79 (¼), 79–81 or 81–79 (½ total) and 81–81 (¼), giving peaks at 158, 160 and 162 in a 1:2:1 ratio. The key idea is that the mixed pair can form two ways, so it is twice as likely as either pure pair.

questions.q: A nuclide lies above the band of stability, with too many neutrons for its number of protons. Which decay mode is most likely?
o: Positron emission
Positron emission raises N/Z, the wrong direction here.
Electron capture
Electron capture also converts p → n, raising N/Z.
Beta-minus emission
Correct: n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino lowers N/Z toward stability.
Gamma emission
Gamma emission does not change N or Z.
questions.x: A neutron-rich nucleus moves toward stability by lowering N/Z. Beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a proton (n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino), doing exactly that. Positron emission and electron capture convert protons into neutrons, which is the fix for proton-rich nuclei below the band, and gamma emission changes neither N nor Z.

questions.q: A beam of radiation passes between charged plates. One part bends slightly toward the negative plate, one bends sharply toward the positive plate, and one is undeflected. What is the sharply bent part?
o: Alpha particles
Alphas are positive and bend toward the negative plate, and only slightly because they are heavy.
Beta-minus particles
Correct: light, negatively charged electrons bend strongly toward the positive plate.
Gamma rays
Gamma rays are uncharged and pass undeflected.
Neutrons
Neutrons are uncharged and would not be deflected.
questions.x: Charged particles bend toward the oppositely charged plate, and lighter particles bend more for a given charge. Beta-minus particles are negative electrons, about 7000 times lighter than alphas, so they bend sharply toward the positive plate. Alphas bend only slightly toward the negative plate, and gamma rays pass undeflected.

questions.q: Electrons emitted in beta-minus decay of a given nuclide have a continuous range of energies rather than one value. What explains this?
o: The nucleus recoils by a random amount
Nuclear recoil is tiny and fixed by momentum conservation in a two-body decay.
Electrons lose varying energy leaving the electron cloud
The spread is present at emission; it is not a shielding effect.
Each nucleus has a different decay energy
Every parent-to-daughter transition has the same Q value.
An antineutrino shares the decay energy
Correct: energy splits among three bodies, so the electron's share varies.
questions.note: This puzzle led Pauli to propose the neutrino.
questions.x: If beta decay produced only an electron and the daughter nucleus, momentum and energy conservation would force one fixed electron energy. The observed continuous spectrum means a third particle, the antineutrino, carries off a variable share of the fixed decay energy. Pauli proposed the neutrino for exactly this reason, and each decay of the same nuclide has the same total energy.

questions.q: After a nucleus decays by electron capture, which emission commonly follows from the atom?
o: X-rays
Correct: outer electrons drop into the inner-shell vacancy, emitting X-ray photons.
Alpha particles
Electron capture does not eject nucleons.
A positron
Positron emission is an alternative to EC, not a consequence of it.
A beta-minus particle
EC lowers Z; β⁻ would reverse that change.
questions.x: Electron capture pulls an inner-shell (usually K-shell) electron into the nucleus, leaving a vacancy. An outer electron drops into that vacancy and releases the energy difference as a characteristic X-ray (or an Auger electron). Nothing else leaves the nucleus besides a neutrino, so alpha or positron emission is not a consequence of capture.

questions.q: In PET imaging, a positron meets an electron and both are annihilated. What is produced?
o: One photon of 511 keV
A single photon cannot conserve momentum from a pair at rest.
Two 511 keV photons traveling in opposite directions
Correct: each photon carries one particle's rest energy, mc² = 511 keV.
A neutron and a neutrino
Annihilation converts mass to photons, not to nucleons.
Two 1.02 MeV photons in the same direction
Doubles the energy and violates momentum conservation.
questions.x: When a positron and electron annihilate nearly at rest, their total rest energy (2 × 511 keV) becomes photons. Since the initial momentum is about zero, the photons must carry equal and opposite momenta, so two 511 keV photons fly apart in opposite directions. PET scanners detect these coincident back-to-back photons to locate the source.

questions.q: A radioactive sample is heated from 25 °C to 500 °C. How does its half-life change?
o: It decreases because decay speeds up when hot
Treats nuclear decay like a chemical reaction with activation energy.
It increases because nuclei become more stable
Thermal energy is far too small to affect nuclear stability.
It doubles for every 10 °C rise
That rule of thumb applies loosely to some chemical reactions only.
It does not change
Correct: nuclear decay rates are independent of temperature and pressure.
questions.x: Radioactive decay depends on nuclear energy levels set by the strong and weak forces, measured in MeV. Thermal energy even at 500 °C is only about 0.1 eV per particle, far too small to affect nuclei, so the half-life stays constant. Temperature dependence via activation energy applies to chemical reactions, not nuclear decay.

questions.q: A rock contains a parent isotope (t½ = 500 million years) and its stable daughter in a daughter-to-parent ratio of 7:1. If all daughter came from the parent, how old is the rock?
o: 500 million years
One half-life gives a 1:1 ratio.
1.0 billion years
Two half-lives gives a 3:1 ratio.
3.5 billion years
Multiplies the ratio 7 by 500 million years.
1.5 billion years
Correct: parent is 1/8 of the original, which is 3 half-lives = 1.5 billion years.
questions.note: Convert D:P to the fraction of parent remaining: P/(P + D).
questions.x: If every daughter atom came from a parent, the original parent count is P + D = 1 + 7 = 8, so 1/8 of the parent remains. That is (1/2)³, or 3 half-lives, giving 3 × 500 million = 1.5 billion years. Multiplying the ratio itself by the half-life skips converting it into a fraction remaining.

questions.q: A hospital needs a tracer for diagnostic imaging that is detected outside the body. Which isotope property is most suitable?
o: Alpha emitter with a half-life of 10 years
Alphas do not escape the body, and a long half-life prolongs exposure.
Beta emitter with a half-life of 2 seconds
Betas are mostly absorbed in tissue, and 2 s is too short to use.
Gamma emitter with a half-life of several hours
Correct: gammas exit the body, and hours allows imaging with little lingering dose.
Stable isotope with no emission
A stable isotope gives no signal for an external detector.
questions.x: An imaging tracer must emit radiation that escapes the body to reach an external detector, which means gamma rays; alphas and betas are absorbed within tissue. Its half-life should be long enough to prepare, inject and image (hours) but short enough that dose does not linger. A 10-year alpha emitter fails both tests and would deposit damaging dose locally.

questions.q: Why does excited hydrogen gas produce a line spectrum instead of a continuous rainbow?
o: Electron energy levels are quantized
Correct: only specific level differences, and so specific photon energies, are possible.
Hydrogen absorbs all visible light
Absorption of all colors would produce darkness, not discrete lines.
The nucleus emits light at fixed frequencies
Visible lines come from electron transitions, not nuclear ones.
Photons of other colors are too fast to detect
All photons travel at c.
questions.x: Electrons in atoms can occupy only discrete energy levels, so a transition can release only a photon whose energy equals a specific level gap. Each allowed gap gives one wavelength, producing bright lines rather than a continuum. A continuous spectrum comes from dense matter such as a hot solid, where energy states are effectively continuous.

questions.q: White light passes through cool sodium vapor and then a prism. What does the spectrum look like?
o: Bright lines on a dark background
That is an emission spectrum from a hot, excited gas.
A continuous spectrum with no features
Ignores that sodium absorbs specific wavelengths.
A continuous spectrum with dark lines at sodium's emission wavelengths
Correct: the gas absorbs exactly the photon energies matching its level gaps.
Dark lines at wavelengths different from sodium's emission lines
Absorption and emission share the same level gaps and so the same wavelengths.
questions.x: Cool gas absorbs exactly the photon energies that match its level gaps, removing those wavelengths from continuous white light. The result is an absorption spectrum: a rainbow with dark lines at the same wavelengths sodium emits when hot, since emission and absorption use the same level gaps. Bright lines on dark only appear when viewing the hot gas itself.

questions.q: Sodium salts give a yellow color in a flame. What produces the light?
o: Sodium nuclei undergoing gamma decay
Gamma rays are not visible light, and sodium-23 is stable.
Combustion of the anion
The characteristic color is the same for many sodium salts, so the cation is responsible.
Excited electrons emitting photons as they drop to lower levels
Correct: the 3p → 3s transition in Na gives the yellow ~589 nm light.
Electrons being removed to form Na⁺
Ionization absorbs energy; it does not emit a fixed color.
