questions.x: Flame heat excites sodium's outer electron from 3s to 3p; as it falls back, it emits a photon near 589 nm, which looks yellow. The color is characteristic of the element because it depends on that atom's level gaps, which is the basis of flame tests. The nucleus is not involved, and ionization absorbs energy rather than emitting a fixed color.

questions.q: An atom absorbs a 500 nm photon, then relaxes in two steps. One emitted photon has a wavelength of 1000 nm. What is the wavelength of the other?
o: 500 nm
Subtracts wavelengths (1000 − 500) instead of energies.
Adds wavelengths (500 + 1000); wavelengths do not add, energies do.
333 nm
Adds 1/λ terms the wrong way; a cascade photon cannot exceed the absorbed energy.
questions.note: Energy (∝ 1/λ) is conserved, not wavelength.
questions.x: Energy is conserved, and photon energy is proportional to 1/λ, so 1/500 = 1/1000 + 1/λ. Solving gives 1/λ = 1/1000, so λ = 1000 nm: the 500 nm photon's energy splits into two equal halves. Wavelengths themselves do not add or subtract, which is the trap.

questions.q: What is the ground-state electron configuration of Cu⁺?
o: [Ar]4s²3d⁸
Ignores both copper's exception and the 4s-first removal rule.
[Ar]3d¹⁰
Correct: Cu is [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰, and the 4s electron is removed first.
[Ar]4s¹3d⁹
Removes a 3d electron instead of the 4s electron.
[Ar]4s²3d⁹
That is the Aufbau-predicted configuration of neutral Cu, with no electron removed.
questions.x: Neutral copper is an exception, [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰, because a filled d subshell is especially stable. When transition metals ionize, the 4s electrons leave before 3d, so Cu⁺ loses its single 4s electron to give [Ar]3d¹⁰. Removing from 3d instead is the common error, since 4s fills first but also empties first.

questions.q: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state Mn²⁺ ion have?
o: Removes electrons from 3d rather than 4s.
Pairs d electrons in violation of Hund's rule.
Correct: Mn²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵, with one electron in each of five d orbitals.
Counts all valence electrons of neutral Mn.
questions.x: Neutral Mn is [Ar]4s²3d⁵, and transition-metal cations lose 4s electrons first, so Mn²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵. By Hund's rule the five d electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, giving 5 unpaired electrons. Removing electrons from 3d instead would leave 3d³ and only 3 unpaired.

questions.q: In a hydrogen atom, the 2s and 2p orbitals have equal energy, but in lithium the 2s is lower. Why?
o: Lithium has more neutrons
Neutrons do not affect orbital energies.
The 2p orbitals in lithium hold more electrons
In ground-state Li the 2p orbitals are empty.
Lithium's nucleus is smaller
Lithium's nucleus is larger and its orbitals are not distorted by nuclear size.
2s penetrates the core, so it is shielded less than 2p
Correct: 2s density near the nucleus raises its Zeff in multi-electron atoms.
questions.x: In hydrogen, with one electron, orbital energy depends only on n. In multi-electron atoms, a 2s electron has some probability density close to the nucleus, inside the 1s core, so it is shielded less and feels a higher effective nuclear charge than a 2p electron. That penetration lowers the 2s energy, producing the familiar s < p < d ordering within a shell.

questions.q: The photoelectron spectrum of a neutral sodium atom shows how many peaks?
o: Correct: one peak per occupied subshell: 1s, 2s, 2p and 3s.
Counts shells rather than subshells.
Peaks correspond to subshells, not individual electrons.
PES detects core electrons too, not only the valence electron.
questions.note: Peak height is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.
questions.x: Photoelectron spectroscopy shows one peak for each occupied subshell, at that subshell's binding energy. Sodium, 1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹, has four occupied subshells, so it gives four peaks, with heights of 2:2:6:1 reflecting electron counts. Counting shells (3) misses that 2s and 2p have different energies.

questions.q: Iron forms Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. Why is Fe³⁺ often especially stable?
o: It has a noble gas configuration
Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵, not [Ar].
It retains both 4s electrons
Both 4s electrons are lost first, in both ions.
It has a half-filled 3d subshell
Correct: [Ar]3d⁵ has five unpaired electrons and extra exchange stability.
It has a filled 3d subshell
A filled 3d subshell would be 3d¹⁰.
questions.x: Iron is [Ar]4s²3d⁶. Losing the two 4s electrons gives Fe²⁺ ([Ar]3d⁶), and losing one more 3d electron gives Fe³⁺ ([Ar]3d⁵). A half-filled d subshell has one electron in each orbital, minimizing repulsion and maximizing exchange energy, which is why Fe³⁺ is so stable. It is not a noble gas configuration.

questions.q: Which element releases the most energy when a gaseous atom gains an electron?
o: F
Fluorine's small 2p shell crowds the added electron, so its EA is less than Cl's.
Br
Br is larger, so the added electron is held less strongly than in Cl.
O
Gaining one electron releases less energy for O than for halogens.
Cl
Correct: Cl has the most negative electron affinity of all elements.
questions.note: Trap: fluorine is the most electronegative but not the highest EA.
questions.x: Electron affinity generally becomes more exothermic toward the halogens, but chlorine, not fluorine, has the most negative value of any element. Fluorine's small 2p shell is crowded, so an added electron feels strong repulsion. Br is larger than Cl and holds the added electron less tightly, and O gains less energy by adding one electron.

questions.q: Zirconium (period 5) and hafnium (period 6) have almost the same atomic radius. What explains this?
o: Lanthanide contraction from poorly shielding 4f electrons
Correct: 14 protons added with weakly shielding 4f electrons offset the new shell.
Hafnium has fewer protons than zirconium
Hafnium (Z = 72) has far more protons than Zr (Z = 40).
Both lack d electrons
Both are d-block metals with d electrons.
Relativistic expansion of hafnium's 6s orbital
Relativity contracts, not expands, heavy-atom s orbitals, and is not the main cause here.
questions.x: Between Zr and Hf, the 4f subshell fills with 14 electrons across the lanthanides. f electrons shield poorly, so the 14 added protons raise effective nuclear charge and contract the atom, offsetting the size gain from the new shell. This lanthanide contraction makes Hf almost the same size as Zr, which is why they are hard to separate chemically.

questions.q: Which species in the isoelectronic set Ne, Na⁺, F⁻, O²⁻ has the highest first ionization energy?
o: Ne
Ne has fewer protons (10) than Na⁺ (11) for the same 10 electrons.
F⁻
Anions hold their extra electrons loosely.
Na⁺
Correct: the most protons pulling on 10 electrons makes removal hardest.
O²⁻
O²⁻ has the fewest protons and the lowest IE.
questions.x: All four species have 10 electrons in the neon configuration, so the one with the most protons holds its electrons most tightly. Na⁺ has 11 protons, more than Ne (10), F⁻ (9) or O²⁻ (8), so removing an electron from it is hardest. Neon being the 'stable noble gas' is the tempting trap.

questions.q: Which aqueous ion is most likely to give a colorless solution?
o: Cu²⁺
Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) has a partly filled d subshell and is blue.
Ni²⁺
Ni²⁺ (3d⁸) allows d–d transitions and is green.
Zn²⁺
Correct: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so no d–d transitions absorb visible light.
Fe³⁺
Fe³⁺ (3d⁵) solutions are typically yellow to brown.
questions.x: Transition-metal ion color usually comes from d–d transitions, in which a d electron absorbs visible light and moves between split d orbitals. Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so every d orbital is full and no d–d transition is possible, leaving the solution colorless. Cu²⁺ (3d⁹), Ni²⁺ (3d⁸) and Fe³⁺ (3d⁵) have partly filled d subshells and are colored.

questions.q: In sodium hydride (NaH), what is the oxidation state of hydrogen?
o: Hydrogen is +1 with more electronegative partners, not with Na.
Correct: Na is less electronegative, so hydrogen gains an electron as hydride, H⁻.
H is bonded, not elemental.
Hydrogen has only one electron to lose.
questions.x: In metal hydrides, hydrogen is more electronegative than the metal partner, so it takes the electron and becomes hydride, H⁻. In NaH, sodium is +1 and hydrogen is −1. The usual +1 for hydrogen applies only when it is bonded to more electronegative atoms, such as in H₂O or HCl.

questions.q: Xenon forms compounds such as XeF₄, but neon forms none. What best explains the difference?
o: Xenon's valence electrons are farther out and have a lower ionization energy
Correct: Xe's outer electrons are easier to share with a very electronegative atom like F.
Xenon has unpaired electrons in its ground state
Xenon's ground state has all electrons paired.
Neon is radioactive
Neon's common isotopes are stable.
Neon has a higher electron affinity
Noble gases have unfavorable electron affinities, and bonding to F requires Xe to share electrons, not gain them.
questions.x: Xenon's valence electrons are in n = 5, far from the nucleus and well shielded, so its ionization energy is low enough for it to share electrons with very electronegative atoms like fluorine. Neon's n = 2 electrons are held extremely tightly. Ground-state xenon has all electrons paired, so bonding is not due to unpaired electrons.

questions.q: Transition metals often show several oxidation states, unlike alkali metals. Why?
o: They have more protons
Proton count alone does not create multiple oxidation states.
Their ns and (n−1)d electrons are close in energy
Correct: varying numbers of s and d electrons can be lost.
They have filled p subshells
Many main-group elements do too, without multiple states.
They are always paramagnetic
Some transition metal species are diamagnetic, and magnetism is unrelated.
questions.x: In transition metals, the ns and (n−1)d orbitals are close in energy, so different numbers of electrons can be removed at similar cost, giving several stable oxidation states (for example Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺). Alkali metals have one valence electron above a noble-gas core, so removing a second electron is far too costly. Proton count and magnetism do not explain this.

questions.q: An unknown solid is shiny, conducts electricity, reacts with water to release H₂, and has a first IE far below its second. Which element fits best?
o: Mg
Mg's first and second IEs are close; the jump is after the second.
Al
Al shows its big jump after the third electron.
Sr
Sr would show its big jump after the second electron.
Na
Correct: a single valence electron gives a large jump after IE1.
questions.x: All four metals are shiny conductors, so the decisive clue is ionization energy. A first IE far below the second means the atom has just one valence electron, and the second must come from a noble-gas core, as in a group 1 metal like sodium, which also reacts with water to release H₂. Group 2 metals (Mg, Sr) show their large jump after IE₂, and Al after IE₃.

questions.q: In a coordinate covalent bond, such as the N–B bond in H₃N–BF₃, the shared electron pair:
o: Is transferred completely to the more electronegative atom
Complete transfer describes ionic bonding, not a shared pair.
Comes entirely from one atom, here the nitrogen lone pair
Correct: the Lewis base (N) donates both electrons to the electron-poor boron.
Comes one electron from each atom, as in any covalent bond
That describes an ordinary covalent bond, not a coordinate one.
Is delocalized over all the fluorine atoms
The pair is localized between N and B; fluorines are not the donor.
questions.note: Coordinate (dative) bond = Lewis base donates both electrons to a Lewis acid.
questions.x: A coordinate (dative) covalent bond forms when a Lewis base donates both electrons of a lone pair to an electron-deficient Lewis acid. In H₃N–BF₃, nitrogen's lone pair fills boron's empty p orbital. Once formed, the bond behaves like any covalent bond, but its electrons originated from one atom rather than one from each, which is the key distinction from an ordinary covalent bond.

questions.q: As two isolated hydrogen atoms approach and form an H₂ molecule, how does the potential energy of the system change?
o: It rises steadily until the bond forms, then stays constant
Bond formation releases energy, so potential energy falls rather than rises.
It stays constant because no electrons are gained or lost
Sharing electrons stabilizes the system; the energy changes.
It decreases continuously the closer the nuclei get
At very short distances nuclear repulsion makes energy rise sharply.
It falls to a minimum at the bond length, then rises sharply if the nuclei get closer
Correct: the minimum marks the equilibrium bond length; its depth is the bond energy.
questions.note: The well depth of the energy curve equals the bond dissociation energy.
questions.x: Two H atoms far apart have zero interaction energy. As they approach, each electron is attracted to both nuclei, lowering the energy until a minimum is reached at the bond length (about 74 pm). Closer than that, nucleus–nucleus repulsion dominates and energy climbs steeply. The depth of this well equals the bond dissociation energy, so energy does not simply keep falling.

questions.q: Which of these molecules does NOT exist because its central atom cannot expand its octet?
o: PCl₅
Phosphorus is in period 3 and can hold more than eight electrons.
SF₄
Sulfur is in period 3 and can expand its octet.
NCl₅
Correct: nitrogen is in period 2 and has no accessible d orbitals, so it cannot exceed an octet.
XeF₂
Xe is in period 5, so it can hold ten electrons (two bonds plus three lone pairs).
questions.note: Only period 3 and lower atoms can have expanded octets.
questions.x: Only atoms in period 3 or below can hold more than eight electrons around them; the usual explanation is that they are larger and have empty d orbitals in their valence shell. Nitrogen is in period 2 with only 2s and 2p orbitals, so it cannot accommodate five bonds and NCl₅ does not exist, though its period-3 analog PCl₅ does. S and Xe, being larger, routinely expand their octets.

questions.q: Using bond energies H–H = 440, Cl–Cl = 240 and H–Cl = 430 kJ/mol, what is ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl?
o: Sign flipped: that is bonds formed minus bonds broken.
Counts only one H–Cl bond formed; two form.
Counts only the two H–Cl bonds formed and ignores the energy needed to break H–H and Cl–Cl.
Correct: ΔH = broken − formed = (440 + 240) − 2(430) = −180 kJ.
questions.note: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
questions.x: Reaction enthalpy can be estimated as energy absorbed breaking bonds minus energy released forming bonds. Breaking one H–H and one Cl–Cl costs 440 + 240 = 680 kJ; forming two H–Cl bonds releases 2 × 430 = 860 kJ. ΔH = 680 − 860 = −180 kJ, exothermic. Reversing the subtraction gives the tempting +180 kJ with the wrong sign.

questions.q: Which Lewis structure contributes most to the cyanate ion, OCN⁻ (C central)?
o: O=C=N with −1 on nitrogen
Reasonable, but the negative charge sits on N rather than the more electronegative O.
O≡C–N with +1 on O and −2 on N
Large, separated formal charges make this a minor contributor.
O=C=N with no formal charges
Impossible: the ion has an overall −1 charge that must appear somewhere.
O–C≡N with −1 on oxygen
Correct: smallest formal charges, with the −1 on the most electronegative atom.
questions.note: Best structure: minimal formal charges, negative charge on the most electronegative atom.
questions.x: Rank resonance contributors by octets first, then by the smallest formal charges, then by placing negative charge on the most electronegative atom. Both O=C=N⁻ (−1 on N) and ⁻O–C≡N (−1 on O) satisfy octets with minimal charge, but oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen and better stabilizes the negative charge. The O≡C–N form with +1 and −2 charges is a minor contributor.

questions.q: Why do many textbooks draw SO₄²⁻ with two S=O bonds rather than four S–O single bonds?
o: It gives sulfur a complete octet, which the single-bond structure lacks
The all-single structure already gives S an octet; the double-bond form expands it.
It reduces the formal charge on sulfur from +2 to 0
Correct: with four single bonds S is +2; two double bonds bring it to 0 and lower charge separation.
It makes the four S–O bonds unequal, as measured experimentally
All four S–O bonds are measured to be equal in length.
It reduces the total number of valence electrons to 30
Electron count is fixed at 32 regardless of the drawing.
questions.note: Formal-charge minimization is the MCAT rationale for expanded octets.
questions.x: With four S–O single bonds, sulfur owns only 4 electrons and has formal charge +2, while every oxygen is −1. Converting two bonds to S=O lets sulfur expand its octet and drops its formal charge to 0, which minimizes charge separation; that is the textbook rationale. The single-bond structure already gives S an octet, so the double bonds do not complete one.

questions.q: How does the bookkeeping for formal charge differ from that for oxidation state?
o: Formal charge gives all bonding electrons to the more electronegative atom
That is the oxidation-state convention.
Formal charge treats bonding electrons as shared equally between the two atoms
Correct: each atom gets half of each bonding pair, ignoring electronegativity.
Formal charge ignores lone pairs
Lone pairs are counted fully toward the atom that holds them.
Formal charge applies only to ions
Neutral molecules such as CO and O₃ have nonzero formal charges.
questions.x: Formal charge assumes perfectly covalent bonds: each atom gets all its lone-pair electrons plus exactly half of every bonding pair, regardless of electronegativity. Oxidation state assumes perfectly ionic bonds: all bonding electrons go to the more electronegative atom. That is why nitrogen in NO₃⁻ has formal charge +1 but oxidation state +5, and why neutral molecules can still carry formal charges.

questions.q: Which species has the longest N–O bonds?
o: NO₂⁺
O=N=O has bond order 2: short bonds.
NO₂⁻
Two resonance structures give bond order 1.5.
NO₃⁻
Correct: three resonance structures give bond order 1⅓, the lowest, so the longest bonds.
NO
Nitric oxide has a bond order above 2: very short.
questions.note: Lower average bond order → longer bond.
questions.x: Bond length increases as bond order decreases. Average bond orders: NO (about 2.5), NO₂⁺ (2, linear O=N=O), NO₂⁻ (1.5 over two resonance structures), NO₃⁻ (4/3, one double bond shared among three oxygens). Nitrate has the lowest bond order and so the longest N–O bonds; nitrite is the tempting choice because it also has resonance, but its bond order is higher.

questions.q: Acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8) is far more acidic than ethanol (pKa ≈ 16). Which factor best explains this?
o: Acetate's negative charge is delocalized over two oxygens by resonance
Correct: resonance stabilizes the conjugate base, so the acid gives up H⁺ more readily.
The O–H bond in acetic acid is a stronger bond
A stronger O–H bond would make the acid weaker, not stronger.
Ethanol has more hydrogen atoms to lose
Acidity depends on conjugate base stability, not the number of hydrogens.
Ethoxide is stabilized by resonance with the methyl group
Ethoxide has no resonance; its charge is localized on one O.
questions.note: More stable conjugate base → stronger acid.
questions.x: Acid strength depends on how stable the conjugate base is. When acetic acid loses H⁺, acetate's negative charge is shared equally between two oxygens by resonance, which strongly stabilizes it. Ethoxide's charge stays localized on one oxygen with no resonance, so ethanol is a much weaker acid. A stronger O–H bond would make an acid weaker, not stronger.

questions.q: The C–N bond in an amide is shorter than a typical C–N single bond, and rotation about it is restricted. What is the best explanation?
o: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl, giving the C–N bond partial double-bond character
Correct: resonance makes the amide planar and the C–N bond partly π.
Nitrogen is sp³ hybridized, which holds substituents rigidly
sp³ nitrogen would allow free rotation; amide N is effectively sp².
Hydrogen bonding between N–H and C=O locks the bond
Restricted rotation exists even in tertiary amides with no N–H.
The carbonyl oxygen sterically blocks rotation
Sterics cannot explain the shortened bond length.
questions.note: This planarity underlies the rigid peptide bond.
questions.x: In an amide, the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the C=O π system, so one resonance contributor has a C=N double bond with negative charge on oxygen. This partial double-bond character shortens the C–N bond, makes the group planar with sp²-like nitrogen, and creates a rotation barrier. Hydrogen bonding cannot be the cause, since tertiary amides with no N–H are equally rigid.

questions.q: For protonated acetone, which resonance contributor is more important: (CH₃)₂C=OH⁺ or (CH₃)₂C⁺–OH?
o: (CH₃)₂C⁺–OH, because the positive charge rests on the less electronegative carbon
Charge placement matters less than complete octets; this carbon has only six electrons.
Both contribute equally because they have the same charge
Equal net charge does not mean equal stability.
(CH₃)₂C=OH⁺, because every atom has a full octet
Correct: full octets outrank placing charge on the less electronegative atom.
Neither, because protonated acetone has no resonance
Moving the π pair onto oxygen gives a valid second structure.
questions.note: Priority: full octets first, then minimal formal charge, then charge on the right atom.
questions.x: When judging resonance contributors, complete octets come first. In (CH₃)₂C=OH⁺ every atom has an octet, and the +1 sits on oxygen. In (CH₃)₂C⁺–OH the positive charge rests on less electronegative carbon, but that carbon has only six electrons. The octet criterion outranks charge placement, so the oxonium form is the major contributor, though the carbocation form explains why the carbon is electrophilic.

questions.q: The H–O–H angle in water is about 104.5°, smaller than the ideal tetrahedral 109.5°. Why?
o: Hydrogen atoms attract each other
Hydrogens bear partial positive charges and repel slightly.
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing the bond angle
Correct: lone pairs occupy more space near O and push the O–H bonds together.
Oxygen is sp² hybridized
Water's oxygen is treated as sp³ with four electron domains.
Hydrogen bonding between molecules bends each molecule
The angle is a property of an isolated molecule, even in the gas phase.
questions.note: Repulsion: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.
questions.x: Water's oxygen has four electron domains (two bonds, two lone pairs), so its ideal electron geometry is tetrahedral at 109.5°. Lone pairs are held only by one nucleus and spread out closer to the central atom, repelling more strongly than bonding pairs. They squeeze the H–O–H angle to about 104.5°. The angle is the same in isolated gas-phase molecules, so hydrogen bonding is not the cause.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of XeF₂?
o: Bent
Bent shapes come from three or four domains with lone pairs; Xe here has five domains.
Linear
Correct: five domains; the three lone pairs fill the equatorial positions, leaving F–Xe–F at 180°.
Trigonal planar
XeF₂ has five domains, not three.
T-shaped
T-shaped needs three bonded atoms.
questions.note: Three equatorial lone pairs on a trigonal bipyramid → linear.
questions.x: Xenon in XeF₂ has two bonds and three lone pairs, five domains with trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry. The three lone pairs occupy the three equatorial positions, 120° apart, which minimizes repulsion. That leaves the two fluorines in the axial positions, directly opposite each other, so the molecule is linear at 180°. Having lone pairs does not always make a molecule bent.

questions.q: Which ranking of bond angles is correct?
o: H₂O > NH₃ > CH₄
Reversed: more lone pairs compress the angle more.
CH₄ > NH₃ > H₂O
Correct: 109.5° > ≈107° > ≈104.5°, as lone pairs increase from 0 to 2.
NH₃ > CH₄ > H₂O
Methane, with no lone pairs, has the largest angle.
All three are 109.5°
Only CH₄ has the ideal angle; lone pairs compress the others.
questions.x: CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O all have four electron domains, so each starts from the 109.5° tetrahedral angle. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so each lone pair squeezes the remaining bonds closer. With 0, 1 and 2 lone pairs, the angles fall from 109.5° to about 107° to about 104.5°. Having the same electron geometry does not mean having the same bond angle.

questions.q: In SF₄, the lone pair on sulfur occupies an equatorial rather than an axial position. Why?
o: Equatorial positions are closer to the nucleus
Position-to-nucleus distances differ only slightly; the deciding factor is the number of 90° neighbors.
Axial positions are reserved for the most electronegative atoms only
Electronegative atoms tend to favor axial sites, but nothing reserves them; lone-pair placement is set by 90° repulsions.
An equatorial lone pair is perpendicular to the π system
SF₄ placement is a VSEPR effect, not a π effect.
An equatorial site has only two 90° neighbors versus three for an axial site
Correct: fewer 90° repulsions minimize energy for the bulky lone pair.
questions.x: In a trigonal bipyramid, repulsions at 90° are far stronger than at 120°. An axial position has three equatorial neighbors at 90°, while an equatorial position has only two (the axial atoms). Lone pairs are bulky and repel most strongly, so they go where they face the fewest 90° contacts: equatorial. That rule produces the seesaw, T-shaped and linear shapes.

questions.q: In pyridine, nitrogen is part of the aromatic ring. What is the hybridization of N, and where is its lone pair?
o: sp³; in an orbital above the ring
Ring atoms in an aromatic system are sp², not sp³.
sp²; in an sp² orbital in the plane of the ring
Correct: the lone pair is not part of the π system, which is why pyridine is basic.
sp²; in the p orbital as part of the aromatic π system
That describes pyrrole; pyridine's N already contributes one p electron.
sp; along the C–N axis
N has three domains, not two.
questions.note: Pyridine's lone pair is available for protonation; pyrrole's is not.
questions.x: Pyridine's nitrogen has three domains (two ring bonds and a lone pair), so it is sp². Its p orbital holds one electron that completes the six-electron aromatic π system, and its lone pair sits in an sp² orbital in the ring plane, pointing outward. Because that pair is not needed for aromaticity, pyridine is basic. In pyrrole, the N lone pair is in the p orbital, so protonating it would destroy aromaticity.

questions.q: In allene, H₂C=C=CH₂, what is the hybridization of the central carbon, and how are the two CH₂ planes oriented?
o: sp²; the two CH₂ groups are coplanar
The central carbon forms two σ bonds and two π bonds: sp.
sp; the two CH₂ groups are coplanar
The two π bonds use perpendicular p orbitals, which twists the ends.
sp²; the two CH₂ groups are perpendicular
sp² would give the central carbon three σ bonds; it has two.
sp; the two CH₂ groups are perpendicular
Correct: the perpendicular p orbitals of the sp carbon force the terminal planes to be at 90°.
questions.x: The central carbon of allene forms two σ bonds, so it is sp and linear. Its two remaining p orbitals are perpendicular: one π bond uses one p orbital with the left carbon, the other uses the second p orbital with the right carbon. Each terminal CH₂ plane must lie perpendicular to the p orbital it overlaps, so the two CH₂ planes end up twisted 90° from each other.

questions.q: How many σ and π bonds are in benzene, C₆H₆?
o: Correct: 6 C–C σ + 6 C–H σ = 12 σ; three π bonds (delocalized) from the alternating doubles.
9 σ, 3 π
Misses three σ bonds; each of six C–C links has a σ bond.
6 σ, 6 π
Ignores the C–H bonds and doubles the π count.
Six π electrons form three π bonds, not six.
questions.note: Count π bonds as pairs of π electrons.
questions.x: Benzene has six C–C links and six C–H bonds, each with one σ bond: 12 σ bonds. Its six π electrons fill three π bonding orbitals, so it is counted as having three π bonds, even though they are delocalized over the whole ring rather than fixed between particular carbons. Counting six π bonds confuses six π electrons with six bonds.

questions.q: NH₃ has a dipole moment of about 1.5 D, but NF₃ has only about 0.2 D, even though N–F bonds are more polar than N–H bonds. Why?
o: In NF₃ the N–F bond dipoles point away from N and oppose the lone-pair dipole
Correct: in NH₃ bond and lone-pair dipoles reinforce; in NF₃ they largely cancel.
NF₃ is trigonal planar, so its dipoles cancel
NF₃ is trigonal pyramidal like NH₃.
Fluorine is less electronegative than nitrogen
Fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen.
NF₃ has no lone pair on nitrogen
N in NF₃ still has one lone pair.
questions.note: Net dipole = vector sum of bond dipoles and lone-pair contributions.
questions.x: A molecule's dipole is the vector sum of bond dipoles and the lone-pair contribution. In NH₃, nitrogen is more electronegative than H, so the bond dipoles point toward N, the same way as the lone pair; they add up. In NF₃, fluorine is more electronegative, so the N–F dipoles point away from N, opposing the lone-pair dipole and nearly canceling it. Both molecules are trigonal pyramidal.

questions.q: A charged rod is held near thin falling streams of four liquids. Which stream is deflected most strongly toward the rod?
o: Hexane
Nonpolar hydrocarbon: no net dipole to align with the field.
Carbon disulfide
Linear S=C=S: bond dipoles cancel.
Dichloromethane
Correct: CH₂Cl₂ has a net dipole, so molecules orient and are pulled toward the charge.
Benzene
Planar and symmetric: no net dipole.
questions.note: Polar molecules align in an electric field; nonpolar ones barely respond.
questions.x: Molecules with a permanent dipole rotate in an electric field so their oppositely charged end faces the rod, and the nonuniform field then pulls them in. Dichloromethane is tetrahedral with two Cl and two H, so its bond dipoles do not cancel. Hexane, CS₂ and benzene have no net dipole, so they respond only weakly through induced dipoles. Polarity comes from symmetry, not just from polar bonds.

questions.q: For molecules of comparable size, which ranking of interaction strengths is typical, from strongest to weakest?
o: Hydrogen bond > ion–dipole > dipole–dipole > London dispersion
Ion–dipole interactions involve full charges and are stronger than H-bonds.
Ion–dipole > hydrogen bond > dipole–dipole > London dispersion
Correct: full charges beat partial ones; H-bonds are especially strong dipole–dipole forces.
Dipole–dipole > hydrogen bond > ion–dipole > London dispersion
Places dipole–dipole above both; H-bonds are the strongest dipole–dipole forces and ion–dipole beats them.
London dispersion > dipole–dipole > hydrogen bond > ion–dipole
This reverses the usual ranking for similar-sized species.
questions.note: Caveat: dispersion can dominate for very large molecules.
questions.x: Interaction strength scales with the charges involved. Ion–dipole forces involve a full ionic charge and are strongest. Hydrogen bonds are especially strong dipole–dipole interactions because H on N, O or F is highly exposed and positive. Ordinary dipole–dipole forces come next, and London dispersion is weakest for molecules of similar size. Very large molecules can still have dispersion forces that dominate.

questions.q: Which hydrogen halide has the lowest boiling point?
o: HF
HF hydrogen bonds and has the highest boiling point of the four.
HCl
Correct: it lacks H-bonding and has the fewest electrons of HCl, HBr and HI, so the weakest dispersion forces.
HBr
More electrons than HCl give stronger dispersion forces.
HI
The largest electron cloud gives the strongest dispersion among HCl–HI.
questions.note: HF is the anomaly; otherwise boiling point rises down the group.
questions.x: Among HCl, HBr and HI, the only attractions are dipole–dipole and dispersion forces, and dispersion grows with the number of electrons, so boiling point rises from HCl (−85 °C) to HI (−35 °C). HF breaks the trend: its H–F bond lets it form strong hydrogen bonds, so it boils near 20 °C despite being the lightest. HCl is therefore lowest.

questions.q: o-Nitrophenol boils at a much lower temperature than p-nitrophenol. What is the best explanation?
o: The ortho isomer has a lower molar mass
The isomers have identical molar masses.
The ortho isomer forms an intramolecular H-bond, leaving fewer intermolecular H-bonds
Correct: the OH and NO₂ groups bond within one molecule, weakening attractions between molecules.
The para isomer is nonpolar
The para isomer has a large dipole and H-bonds intermolecularly.
The ortho isomer cannot hydrogen bond at all
It does hydrogen bond, but internally.
questions.note: Intramolecular H-bonds lower boiling points relative to isomers.
questions.x: In o-nitrophenol, the OH and NO₂ groups are adjacent, so the OH hydrogen bonds to a nitro oxygen within the same molecule, forming a six-membered ring. With its donor tied up internally, the molecule forms few hydrogen bonds to neighbors, so it is more volatile. In p-nitrophenol the groups are too far apart, so OH hydrogen bonds to other molecules, raising the boiling point. Both isomers have identical mass.

questions.q: Propane (C₃H₈), acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) and ethanol (C₂H₅OH) have similar molar masses (44–46 g/mol). Which order lists them by increasing boiling point?
o: Ethanol < acetaldehyde < propane
Reversed: stronger intermolecular forces raise boiling point.
Acetaldehyde < propane < ethanol
Propane, with only dispersion forces, boils lowest.
Propane < acetaldehyde < ethanol
Correct: dispersion only < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding.
Propane < ethanol < acetaldehyde
Acetaldehyde cannot donate H-bonds, so it boils below ethanol.
questions.note: At similar mass, rank by the strongest IMF available.
questions.x: At similar molar mass, dispersion forces are comparable, so boiling point is set by the strongest additional interaction. Propane is nonpolar with only dispersion forces and boils near −42 °C. Acetaldehyde has a polar C=O and adds dipole–dipole attraction, boiling near 20 °C. Ethanol can donate and accept hydrogen bonds and boils at 78 °C. Acetaldehyde has an oxygen but no O–H, so it cannot match ethanol.

questions.q: In ethane, H₃C–CH₃, each C–H σ bond forms from the overlap of which orbitals?
o: A carbon 2p orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
Unhybridized p orbitals cannot give four equivalent bonds at 109.5°.
A carbon sp² orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
sp² carbons have three domains; each ethane carbon has four σ bonds.
A carbon sp³ orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
Correct: each tetrahedral carbon uses sp³ hybrids, and hydrogen uses its only valence orbital, 1s.
A carbon sp³ orbital and a hydrogen sp³ orbital
Hydrogen has only a 1s orbital and does not hybridize.
questions.x: Each carbon in ethane forms four σ bonds arranged tetrahedrally, so it is sp³ hybridized. Every C–H bond is head-on overlap of one carbon sp³ hybrid with hydrogen's 1s orbital, and the C–C bond is sp³–sp³ overlap. Hydrogen has only one valence orbital, 1s, so it never hybridizes. Pure p orbitals would give 90° bonds, not the observed 109.5°.

questions.q: At 25 °C, which liquid has the highest vapor pressure?
o: Water
Strong hydrogen bonding keeps molecules in the liquid.
Diethyl ether
Correct: no H-bond donors, so weak IMFs let molecules escape easily.
Ethanol
Ethanol hydrogen bonds, lowering its vapor pressure.
Glycerol
Three OH groups make glycerol's vapor pressure very low.
questions.note: Weaker IMFs → higher vapor pressure → lower boiling point.
questions.x: Vapor pressure measures how easily molecules escape from the liquid, so weaker intermolecular forces mean higher vapor pressure. Diethyl ether has no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself and is held only by weak dipole and dispersion forces, giving it very high vapor pressure (bp 35 °C). Ethanol, water and glycerol all hydrogen bond, with glycerol's three OH groups giving the lowest vapor pressure.

questions.q: Acetic acid (60 g/mol, bp 118 °C) boils higher than 1-propanol (60 g/mol, bp 97 °C). What is the best explanation?
o: Acetic acid has more electrons, so stronger dispersion forces
The molar masses and electron counts are nearly equal.
1-Propanol cannot hydrogen bond
1-Propanol has an OH group and does hydrogen bond.
Acetic acid ionizes completely in the pure liquid
Pure acetic acid is barely ionized.
Acetic acid pairs form two hydrogen bonds each (dimers) and the C=O adds strong polarity
Correct: the carboxyl group both donates and accepts, forming strongly H-bonded dimers.
questions.note: Carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols of similar mass.
questions.x: Both compounds have the same molar mass and can hydrogen bond. The carboxyl group of acetic acid contains both an O–H donor and a C=O acceptor, so two molecules pair into a cyclic dimer held by two hydrogen bonds, and the polar C=O adds strong dipole attraction. These interactions exceed those of 1-propanol's single OH, so the acid boils about 20 °C higher. Pure acetic acid is barely ionized.

questions.q: SiO₂ melts above 1600 °C, but CO₂ sublimes at −78 °C. What explains this difference?
o: SiO₂ is ionic and CO₂ is covalent
SiO₂ is covalently bonded, not ionic.
Si–O bonds are polar and C=O bonds are not
Both bond types are polar.
CO₂ is linear, so it has no intermolecular forces at all
CO₂ still has dispersion forces, just weak ones.
SiO₂ is a network solid whose melting breaks covalent bonds; CO₂ is held only by weak intermolecular forces
Correct: melting quartz requires breaking Si–O bonds throughout the lattice.
questions.note: Network covalent solids (diamond, quartz) have the highest melting points.
questions.x: Despite similar formulas, SiO₂ and CO₂ have very different structures. Silicon does not form stable π bonds with oxygen, so each Si bonds to four O atoms in a continuous three-dimensional network; melting quartz requires breaking strong Si–O covalent bonds. CO₂ is a discrete linear molecule held to its neighbors only by weak dispersion forces, so it sublimes at −78 °C. Both contain polar covalent bonds.

questions.q: Sodium stearate (a soap) forms micelles in water. How are the molecules arranged?
o: Nonpolar tails point inward and charged heads face the water
Correct: tails avoid water while carboxylate heads interact with it.
Charged heads point inward and tails face the water
That is a reverse micelle, which forms in nonpolar solvents.
Molecules stack in a flat bilayer sheet
Single-tailed soaps favor spherical micelles, not bilayers.
Molecules dissolve individually with no organization
Above the critical concentration they aggregate.
questions.note: The hydrophobic effect drives micelle formation.
questions.x: Soap molecules are amphipathic: a long nonpolar hydrocarbon tail and a charged carboxylate head. In water, the tails cluster inside a sphere, away from water, while the heads face outward and interact with water through ion–dipole forces. The hydrophobic effect drives this, because it frees water from ordering around tails. Reversed arrangements form only in nonpolar solvents, and double-tailed lipids prefer bilayers.

questions.q: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, and why: NaF or NaI?
o: NaI, because iodide has more electrons
More electrons do not strengthen ionic attraction; larger size weakens it.
NaI, because I⁻ is more polarizable
Polarizability matters for dispersion, not lattice energy here.
NaF, because the smaller F⁻ lets the ions get closer
Correct: smaller interionic distance means stronger Coulomb attraction.
They are equal, because both ions have the same charges
Same charges, but different ion sizes change the distance.
questions.x: NaF and NaI have the same ion charges, so lattice energy depends on interionic distance. Fluoride is much smaller than iodide, so Na⁺ and F⁻ sit closer together, and Coulomb attraction, proportional to 1/r, is stronger. NaF therefore has the larger lattice energy and a higher melting point. Iodide's greater size and polarizability do not strengthen ionic attraction.

questions.q: Why are ionic crystals brittle, shattering when struck?
o: Their covalent bonds are weak
Ionic crystals are held by ionic attractions, not covalent bonds.
Electrons flow away from the impact site
Ionic solids have no mobile electrons.
Ions are only weakly attracted to each other
Ionic attractions are strong; that is why melting points are high.
Shifting a layer brings like charges side by side, and they repel
Correct: displacement aligns cations with cations and anions with anions.
questions.note: Contrast: metals deform because their electron sea moves with the ions.
questions.x: In an ionic crystal, each ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge. A sharp blow that shifts one layer by half an ion spacing places cations next to cations and anions next to anions; these like charges repel strongly and the crystal cleaves along that plane. Ionic attractions are strong, which is why melting points are high; brittleness comes from the geometry of repulsion, not weak bonding.

questions.q: Which bond has the greatest ionic character?
o: Cs–F
Correct: the least electronegative metal with the most electronegative nonmetal gives the largest ΔEN.
Li–I
Small Li⁺ and large I⁻ have a smaller ΔEN and significant covalent character.
Na–Cl
Ionic, but ΔEN is smaller than for Cs–F.
Be–Cl
Beryllium chloride is largely covalent.
questions.x: Ionic character increases with the electronegativity difference between the two atoms. Cesium is among the least electronegative elements (about 0.8) and fluorine is the most electronegative (4.0), so Cs–F has the largest difference, above 3. Na–Cl is also ionic but has a smaller difference, while small, highly polarizing cations such as Li⁺ and Be²⁺ give Li–I and Be–Cl substantial covalent character.

questions.q: Butane and 2-methylpropane (isobutane), both C₄H₁₀, are best described as:
o: Enantiomers
Enantiomers have the same connectivity and are mirror images.
Diastereomers
Diastereomers have the same connectivity.
Conformers
Conformers interconvert by bond rotation; these require bond breaking.
Constitutional (structural) isomers
Correct: same formula, different atom connectivity.
questions.x: Butane (a straight four-carbon chain) and isobutane (three carbons with a methyl branch on the middle carbon) share the formula C₄H₁₀ but connect their atoms differently, making them constitutional isomers. Stereoisomers, which include enantiomers and diastereomers, share connectivity and differ only in 3-D arrangement. Conformers interconvert by single-bond rotation, while turning butane into isobutane requires breaking bonds.

questions.q: Which method can separate a racemic mixture into its two enantiomers?
o: Simple distillation
Enantiomers have identical boiling points.
Extraction with water
Enantiomers have identical solubility in achiral solvents.
Reaction with a single enantiomer of a chiral acid, then crystallization
Correct: this forms diastereomeric salts with different physical properties.
Standard silica gel chromatography
An achiral stationary phase cannot distinguish enantiomers.
questions.note: Resolution converts enantiomers into separable diastereomers.
questions.x: Enantiomers have identical physical properties in an achiral environment, so distillation, extraction and ordinary chromatography cannot separate them. Reacting the racemic acid or base with one pure enantiomer of a chiral resolving agent converts the pair into diastereomeric salts, such as (R,R) and (S,R), which differ in solubility and can be separated by crystallization. The resolving agent is then removed to recover each enantiomer.

questions.q: A pure enantiomer has specific rotation +20°. A mixture of it and its enantiomer has specific rotation +6°. What percentage of the mixture is the (+) enantiomer?
o: That is the enantiomeric excess, not the percentage of (+).
That is the racemic portion of the mixture.
That is the percentage of the (−) enantiomer.
questions.note: ee = observed ÷ pure rotation; major = ee + (100 − ee)/2.
questions.x: Enantiomeric excess equals observed rotation divided by the pure enantiomer's rotation: 6/20 = 0.30, or 30%. That means 30% of the sample is excess (+) and the other 70% is racemic, split evenly as 35% (+) and 35% (−). So (+) = 30% + 35% = 65% and (−) = 35%. Reporting 30% confuses the excess with the actual percentage of the major enantiomer.

questions.q: Diethyl ether (density 0.71 g/mL) is shaken with water in a separatory funnel. Where is the ether layer?
o: On top, because it is less dense than water
Correct: immiscible layers stack by density, and ether is less dense than water.
On the bottom, because organic layers always sink
Organic layers sink only when denser than water, as with dichloromethane.
On top, because it is more polar than water
Layer position depends on density, and ether is far less polar than water.
Mixed evenly through the water as one phase
Ether and water are largely immiscible and form two layers.
questions.x: In a separatory funnel, two immiscible liquids stack by density: the less dense one floats. Diethyl ether (0.71 g/mL) is lighter than water (1.00 g/mL), so it is the top layer. Polarity decides whether liquids mix, not which one sits on top, and many organic solvents (ether, hexane, ethyl acetate) float, while halogenated ones sink.

questions.q: A product is extracted from water into dichloromethane (density 1.33 g/mL). Which layer should be drained and kept?
o: The top layer, which is the organic phase
Assumes all organic solvents float; dichloromethane is denser than water.
The bottom layer, which is the aqueous phase
Water (1.00 g/mL) is less dense than dichloromethane, so it sits on top.
Either layer, since the product splits evenly
A neutral organic product partitions strongly into the organic layer.
The bottom layer, which is the organic phase
Correct: dichloromethane is denser than water, so the organic layer is on the bottom.
questions.note: Trap: halogenated solvents like CH₂Cl₂ and CHCl₃ sink below water.
questions.x: Layer position depends only on density. Dichloromethane (1.33 g/mL) is denser than water, so the organic layer is on the bottom and is drained out through the stopcock. A neutral organic product partitions into that layer. The tempting mistake is assuming the organic layer is always on top, which holds only for solvents less dense than water.

questions.q: An ether solution contains p-cresol (a phenol, pKa ≈ 10) and naphthalene. Which aqueous wash moves p-cresol into the water layer?
o: Saturated NaHCO₃
Bicarbonate (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 6.4) is too weak a base to deprotonate a phenol.
1 M NaOH
Correct: hydroxide fully deprotonates the phenol to a water-soluble phenoxide.
1 M HCl
Acid keeps the phenol neutral, so it stays in the ether.
Saturated NaCl
Brine removes water from the organic layer; it does not ionize the phenol.
questions.note: NaHCO₃ removes carboxylic acids only; NaOH removes carboxylic acids and phenols.
questions.x: A base moves an acid into water only if it is strong enough to deprotonate it: the base's conjugate acid must have a higher pKa than the acid being removed. Hydroxide (conjugate acid water, pKa ≈ 15.7) easily deprotonates a phenol (pKa ≈ 10), making a charged phenoxide that dissolves in water. Bicarbonate (pKa ≈ 6.4) is too weak for phenols and removes only carboxylic acids.

questions.q: In the sequence NaHCO₃ wash then NaOH wash of an ether solution of benzoic acid, 2-naphthol and naphthalene, what is in the NaOH extract?
o: Benzoic acid as sodium benzoate
Benzoic acid was removed by the earlier bicarbonate wash.
Naphthalene
Naphthalene has no acidic proton and stays in ether.
2-Naphthol as its sodium salt
Correct: the carboxylic acid was already removed by bicarbonate, leaving only the phenol for NaOH.
Both benzoate and naphthoxide
Possible only if NaOH were used first; the weak base went first here.
questions.note: Use the weaker base first to separate a carboxylic acid from a phenol.
questions.x: Using bases in order of increasing strength separates acids by pKa. Bicarbonate is strong enough for a carboxylic acid (pKa ≈ 4 to 5) but not a phenol (pKa ≈ 10), so the first wash removes only benzoic acid. The later NaOH wash then takes the 2-naphthol as sodium naphthoxide. If NaOH were used first, it would remove both acids together.

questions.q: For a fixed total volume of extracting solvent, which approach recovers the most solute from water?
o: One extraction with the whole volume
One large extraction leaves more solute behind than several smaller ones.
Either approach, since total solvent volume is equal
Partitioning is not linear in volume; splitting it improves recovery.
One extraction followed by heating the funnel
Heating a closed funnel with volatile solvent is hazardous and does not aid partitioning.
Several extractions with smaller portions
Correct: each portion removes a fraction of what remains, so repeated small extractions beat one large one.
questions.x: In each extraction, a fixed fraction of the remaining solute moves into the fresh solvent. Several small portions apply that fraction repeatedly, so the amount left behind shrinks geometrically and total recovery beats one large portion of the same total volume. Partitioning is not linear in solvent volume, which is why splitting the volume helps.

questions.q: Same solute (K = 4), 1.0 g in 100 mL of water, but now extracted twice with 50 mL organic portions. About how much is extracted in total?
o: This is only the first 50 mL extraction (2/3 of the solute).
That is the single 100 mL extraction result; two portions do better.
Correct: each 50 mL pass leaves 1/3 behind, so (1/3)² = 1/9 remains and 8/9 ≈ 0.89 g is extracted.
Partitioning never removes all solute in a finite number of extractions.
questions.x: The fraction left in water after each extraction is Vaq/(Vaq + K·Vorg) = 100/(100 + 4×50) = 1/3. After two extractions (1/3)² = 1/9 of the solute remains, so about 8/9 ≈ 0.89 g is extracted, more than the 0.80 g from one 100 mL portion. Recovery approaches but never reaches 100% in a finite number of extractions.

questions.q: How does a fractionating column improve separation compared with simple distillation?
o: It raises the boiling point of the less volatile component
A column does not change intrinsic boiling points.
It cools the vapor so it condenses faster
Condensing is the condenser's job; the column's job is repeated equilibration.
It filters nonvolatile impurities from the vapor
Nonvolatile impurities never vaporize; the column enriches volatile components.
It provides many successive vaporization–condensation cycles
Correct: each cycle (theoretical plate) further enriches the vapor in the more volatile component.
questions.x: A fractionating column offers a large surface on which vapor repeatedly condenses and re-vaporizes. Each cycle is like a separate simple distillation (a theoretical plate), enriching the vapor further in the more volatile component. The column does not change any compound's boiling point; it multiplies the separation.

questions.q: A compound boils at 280 °C at 1 atm but decomposes near 250 °C. Why is vacuum distillation used to purify it?
o: The vacuum raises its vapor pressure at every temperature
Vapor pressure at a given temperature is an intrinsic property, unaffected by the applied vacuum.
The vacuum removes oxygen, which is the only cause of decomposition
Thermal decomposition can occur without oxygen; the key is the lower temperature.
Lowering the pressure lowers its boiling point below the decomposition temperature
Correct: a liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure, so less pressure means a lower bp.
Reduced pressure increases the difference between boiling points
The main purpose is to lower the boiling temperature.
questions.x: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure. Lowering the pressure with a vacuum means the compound reaches that vapor pressure at a lower temperature, so it can be distilled below 250 °C without decomposing. The vacuum does not change the compound's vapor pressure at a given temperature; it lowers the pressure the vapor must match.

questions.q: Fractional distillation of dilute aqueous ethanol stops enriching at about 95.6% ethanol no matter how efficient the column. Why?
o: Ethanol and water have identical boiling points
Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C.
The mixture forms an azeotrope whose vapor and liquid have the same composition
Correct: at the azeotrope, vaporization no longer changes composition, so distillation cannot enrich further.
The column runs out of theoretical plates
Even unlimited plates cannot pass an azeotropic composition.
Water reacts with ethanol at its boiling point
No reaction occurs; the limit is a vapor–liquid equilibrium effect.
questions.x: Ethanol and water form a minimum-boiling azeotrope at about 95.6% ethanol. At that composition the vapor has the same composition as the liquid, so further vaporization–condensation cycles cannot enrich it. More theoretical plates do not help; getting past an azeotrope needs a different method, such as a drying agent or adding a third component.

questions.q: An ideal 50:50 (mole) liquid mixture has P°A = 300 torr and P°B = 100 torr. What is the mole fraction of A in the vapor?
o: The vapor is enriched in the more volatile component, not equal to the liquid.
Computes 300/(300 + 150) or another mix-up; use the partial pressures 150 and 50 torr.
Overestimates enrichment; Raoult's law gives 150/200.
questions.note: Raoult's law: Pᵢ = xᵢP°ᵢ, then yᵢ = Pᵢ/P(total).
questions.x: Raoult's law gives each partial pressure as Pᵢ = xᵢP°ᵢ: PA = 0.5 × 300 = 150 torr and PB = 0.5 × 100 = 50 torr. The vapor mole fraction is yA = PA/Ptotal = 150/200 = 0.75. The vapor is always richer than the liquid in the more volatile component, which is the basis of distillation.

questions.q: During fractional distillation of a two-liquid mixture, the head temperature holds steady, then rises sharply before leveling off again. What does the sharp rise indicate?
o: The column has flooded and must be emptied
Flooding disrupts flow; it does not produce a clean plateau-to-plateau transition.
An azeotrope has formed in the pot
An azeotrope would distill at a constant temperature, not cause a jump.
The higher-boiling component is decomposing
Decomposition is not indicated by a clean transition to a new plateau.
The lower-boiling component has largely distilled over
Correct: once the volatile component is depleted, the vapor temperature climbs toward the second boiling point.
questions.note: Change receivers during the temperature jump to keep fractions pure.
questions.x: A temperature plateau at the head means one component is distilling at its boiling point. When that lower-boiling component is used up, the vapor temperature rises until the higher-boiling component begins to distill at a new plateau. Changing receivers during the rise keeps each fraction pure. An azeotrope would distill at one constant temperature.

questions.q: A hot recrystallization solution contains insoluble dust particles. What should be done next?
o: Cool the solution in ice, then vacuum-filter the mixture
The dust would be collected along with the crystals.
Add more solvent until the dust dissolves
Insoluble impurities will not dissolve, and excess solvent lowers yield.
Gravity-filter the solution while hot, then cool the filtrate
Correct: hot gravity filtration removes insolubles while keeping the product dissolved.
Add activated charcoal to dissolve the dust
Charcoal adsorbs colored impurities; it does not dissolve particles.
questions.x: Insoluble impurities are removed by filtering the solution while it is still hot, so the desired compound stays dissolved and passes through. Gravity filtration with fluted paper is used, because vacuum would cool the solution and cause early crystallization in the funnel. If the solution were cooled first, the dust would be collected along with the crystals.

questions.q: Compound X dissolves to 20 g/100 mL at 80 °C and 2 g/100 mL at 0 °C. If 10 g of X is dissolved in 50 mL of hot solvent and cooled to 0 °C, what is the maximum recovery?
o: 8 g
Uses 2 g lost per 50 mL; at 2 g/100 mL, 50 mL holds only 1 g.
9 g
Correct: 50 mL holds 1 g at 0 °C, so 10 − 1 = 9 g can crystallize.
Some compound always remains dissolved in the cold solvent.
5 g
Halves the mass without using the cold solubility data.
questions.x: At 0 °C the solvent holds 2 g per 100 mL, so 50 mL keeps 1 g dissolved. The rest, 10 − 1 = 9 g, can crystallize, which is the maximum recovery. First check that all 10 g dissolve hot: 50 mL holds 10 g at 80 °C, so it does. Using 2 g as the loss ignores that only 50 mL of solvent is present.

questions.q: Purified crystals are usually collected after recrystallization by:
o: Simple distillation
Distillation separates liquids by volatility, not solids from liquids.
Vacuum filtration with a Büchner funnel
Correct: suction quickly pulls off mother liquor and partly dries the crystals.
Gravity filtration through fluted paper
Gravity filtration is slower and used when the filtrate is wanted or the solution is hot.
Liquid–liquid extraction
Extraction partitions solutes between liquids; it does not collect solids.
questions.x: Vacuum filtration through a Büchner funnel quickly separates crystals from the mother liquor and pulls air through the solid to partly dry it. It is the standard method when the solid is the product. Gravity filtration is slower and is used when the liquid is the desired part or the solution must stay hot.

questions.q: An alcohol (Rf 0.25 on silica) is oxidized to a ketone. After 1 hour, the reaction lane shows spots at Rf 0.25 and 0.55. What is the best interpretation?
o: The reaction is complete, and the ketone is the lower spot
The lower spot matches the starting alcohol.
The reaction is incomplete, and the less polar ketone is the upper spot
Correct: the ketone loses the O–H and moves farther, while remaining alcohol stays at 0.25.
The ketone is more polar than the alcohol and runs at 0.25
Losing hydrogen bonding makes the ketone less polar, giving it a higher Rf.
Two side products formed and no starting material remains
The spot at 0.25 matches the starting material.
questions.x: On silica, more polar compounds have lower Rf. An alcohol can hydrogen bond to silica through its O–H, while the ketone product cannot donate a hydrogen bond, so the ketone is less polar and runs higher (Rf 0.55). The spot remaining at 0.25 matches the starting alcohol, so the reaction is not yet complete.

questions.q: An unknown and an authentic sample give identical Rf values in one solvent system. What is the best additional evidence that they are the same compound?
o: Rerunning both in the same eluent gives the same Rf again
Repeating the same conditions cannot distinguish compounds with coincidentally equal Rf.
Both spots appear under UV light
Many different compounds absorb UV.
Both spots have the same size
Spot size reflects amount applied, not identity.
A co-spot gives a single spot in a second, different eluent
Correct: matching in multiple solvent systems and co-spotting rules out coincidental Rf matches.
questions.x: Different compounds can have the same Rf in one solvent by coincidence, so one match is weak evidence. Co-spotting puts the unknown and the authentic sample in the same lane, where two different compounds would usually show two spots or an elongated spot. Repeating this in a second, different eluent makes a coincidental match much less likely.

questions.q: On silica TLC, a target compound has Rf 0.00 in pure hexane and 0.95 in pure ethyl acetate. What is the best eluent for column purification?
o: Pure hexane
The compound would never leave the column.
Pure ethyl acetate
The compound would race through near the solvent front with poor separation.
A hexane/ethyl acetate mixture giving the target Rf ≈ 0.3
Correct: moderate Rf gives enough retention to separate from impurities while still eluting.
Water
Water is not a practical silica eluent and would deactivate the silica.
questions.x: A good column eluent puts the target at an Rf of about 0.2 to 0.4 on TLC. That gives enough retention to separate the target from impurities but still elutes it in a reasonable volume. At Rf 0 it never leaves the column, and near Rf 1 it runs with the solvent front and separates poorly, so a hexane/ethyl acetate mix in between is best.

questions.q: A carboxylic acid (pKa 4.5) is analyzed by reverse-phase HPLC. The mobile phase pH is lowered from 7 to 2.5. What happens to its retention time?
o: It decreases, because the acid becomes ionized
At pH 2.5 the acid is mostly protonated, not ionized.
It increases, because the neutral acid binds the C18 phase more strongly
Correct: below its pKa the acid is mostly protonated and less polar, so it is retained longer.
It is unchanged, because pH does not affect reverse phase
Ionization state strongly affects hydrophobic retention.
It decreases, because the C18 phase becomes charged
C18 chains carry no ionizable groups.
questions.note: Neutral forms are retained longer in reverse phase than ionized forms.
questions.x: Reverse-phase retention depends on hydrophobicity, and ionized molecules are much more polar than neutral ones. At pH 7, well above the pKa of 4.5, the acid is mostly a polar carboxylate that elutes early. At pH 2.5, two units below the pKa, it is about 99% neutral RCOOH, which binds C18 more strongly, so its retention time increases.

questions.q: A protein runs as a single 50 kDa band on SDS-PAGE but elutes from a calibrated gel filtration column at about 200 kDa. What is the best interpretation?
o: The protein is degraded during gel filtration
Degradation would make it appear smaller, not larger.
SDS adds 150 kDa of mass to the protein
SDS binding does not change the apparent mass on gel filtration.
The native protein is a tetramer of identical subunits
Correct: SDS-PAGE gives subunit mass, gel filtration gives native size: 200/50 = 4.
The protein is a monomer with four disulfide bonds
Disulfides within one chain do not quadruple native size.
questions.x: SDS-PAGE denatures proteins and breaks apart noncovalent subunits, so it reports the mass of a single polypeptide (50 kDa). Gel filtration is run under native conditions and measures the size of the intact assembly (about 200 kDa). The ratio 200/50 = 4 shows a tetramer of identical subunits. Disulfides within one chain cannot change the total mass.

questions.q: Proteins with pI 4.5, 6.5 and 9.0 are loaded onto a DEAE (anion-exchange) column at pH 7.5. Which protein flows through without binding?
o: The protein with pI 9.0
Correct: at pH 7.5 it is net positive and is repelled by the positive DEAE groups.
The protein with pI 4.5
It is strongly negative at pH 7.5 and binds tightly.
The protein with pI 6.5
It is mildly negative at pH 7.5 and binds.
None of them binds the column
Proteins with pI below 7.5 are negative and bind DEAE.
questions.x: DEAE is an anion exchanger with positive groups, so it binds proteins that are net negative, which means the buffer pH is above their pI. At pH 7.5, the proteins with pI 4.5 and 6.5 are negative and bind. For the pI 9.0 protein, pH 7.5 is below its pI, so it is net positive, is repelled, and flows through.

questions.q: Proteins with pI 4.5 and 6.5 are bound to DEAE at pH 7.5 and eluted with an increasing NaCl gradient. Which elutes last?
o: The protein with pI 6.5
Being less negative, it is displaced at lower salt.
Both elute together
Different net charges give different binding strengths.
The protein with pI 4.5
Correct: it carries more negative charge at pH 7.5, so it binds more tightly and needs more salt.
Neither elutes with salt
Salt competes for charged sites and elutes bound proteins.
questions.x: On an anion exchanger, the more negative a protein's net charge, the more tightly it binds and the more salt it takes to elute it. At pH 7.5, the protein with pI 4.5 is three units above its pI and carries more negative charge than the pI 6.5 protein. It therefore elutes last, at the highest salt.

questions.q: Uncut plasmid DNA shows three bands: supercoiled, nicked circular and linear forms of the same length. Which form typically migrates fastest?
o: Supercoiled
Correct: its compact, twisted shape moves through agarose most easily.
Nicked (relaxed) circular
The open, floppy circle experiences the most drag and is usually slowest.
Linear
Linear DNA usually runs between supercoiled and nicked forms.
All migrate equally, since they have equal mass
Shape affects mobility, not just mass.
questions.x: Plasmid forms with the same length have the same mass and charge, so their mobility depends on shape. Supercoiled DNA is tightly twisted and compact, so it slips through the gel most easily and usually runs fastest. Nicked circles are open and floppy and run slowest, and linear DNA usually runs in between.

questions.q: On an agarose gel, a 1000 bp marker runs 4 cm and a 100 bp marker runs 8 cm. Migration distance is linear in log(size). About how large is a fragment that runs 6 cm?
o: 550 bp
Assumes size is linear with distance, not log(size).
300 bp
Correct: 6 cm is halfway in log scale, 10^2.5 ≈ 316 bp.
200 bp
Underestimates; the log midpoint of 100 and 1000 is about 316.
750 bp
Places the fragment too close to the 1000 bp marker.
questions.note: Use log(size) vs distance for gel standards.
questions.x: Over a gel's useful range, migration distance is roughly linear in the logarithm of fragment size. Here 4 cm corresponds to log 1000 = 3 and 8 cm to log 100 = 2, so 6 cm corresponds to log size = 2.5, which is 10^2.5 ≈ 316 bp, or about 300 bp. Assuming size itself is linear with distance gives the wrong answer of 550 bp.

questions.q: An antibody runs at about 150 kDa on nonreducing SDS-PAGE but gives bands at about 50 and 25 kDa when β-mercaptoethanol is added. What explains this?
o: SDS breaks peptide bonds under reducing conditions
Neither SDS nor β-mercaptoethanol hydrolyzes peptide bonds.
The chains are held by noncovalent forces only
SDS alone would then separate them, even without reducing agent.
β-Mercaptoethanol removes carbohydrate from the antibody
It reduces disulfides; it does not deglycosylate.
Heavy and light chains are held together by disulfide bonds
Correct: reducing agent breaks interchain disulfides, releasing 50 kDa heavy and 25 kDa light chains.
questions.x: SDS breaks noncovalent interactions, but disulfide bonds survive unless a reducing agent like β-mercaptoethanol is added. An IgG antibody has two heavy and two light chains joined by interchain disulfides, so it runs intact at about 150 kDa without reduction. Reduction releases separate heavy (about 50 kDa) and light (about 25 kDa) chains.

questions.q: Two globular proteins of 60 kDa have pI values of 5.0 and 6.5. They are run on native PAGE at pH 8.8 toward the anode. Which migrates farther?
o: The protein with pI 6.5
It is less negatively charged at pH 8.8.
The protein with pI 5.0
Correct: farther below its pI, it carries more negative charge at pH 8.8 and moves faster.
Both migrate equally, since they have equal mass
Native PAGE depends on charge and shape, not just mass.
Neither enters the gel
Both are negative at pH 8.8 and move toward the anode.
questions.x: In native PAGE, mobility depends on net charge and size and shape. At pH 8.8 both proteins are above their pI and are negative, but the protein with pI 5.0 is farther below the buffer pH and carries more negative charge. With equal mass and similar shape, the more highly charged protein moves farther toward the anode.

questions.q: Two forms of a protein differ only by a single phosphate group. In 2D gel electrophoresis (IEF then SDS-PAGE), how are they best distinguished?
o: By a shift in the IEF dimension toward lower pI
Correct: the added negative phosphate lowers the pI, while the mass change is too small to resolve by SDS-PAGE.
By a large shift in the SDS-PAGE dimension
About 80 Da is negligible relative to protein mass.
By a shift toward higher pI
Adding a negatively charged group lowers pI.
They cannot be separated in 2D gels
IEF readily resolves charge isoforms.
questions.x: A phosphate group adds negative charge, which lowers a protein's pI, so the phosphorylated form focuses at a slightly more acidic position in the IEF dimension. Its mass rises by only about 80 Da, which is too small to resolve by SDS-PAGE for a typical protein. 2D gels therefore show phosphoforms as a horizontal row of spots at nearly the same size.

questions.q: Glycine (pI ≈ 6.0) is placed in an electric field in a buffer at pH 3. Which way does it migrate?
o: Toward the anode
That occurs at pH above the pI, where glycine is net negative.
It does not move
It is stationary only at pH = pI.
It splits evenly toward both electrodes
Rapid proton exchange gives every molecule the same average positive charge, so all move the same way.
Toward the cathode
Correct: below its pI, glycine carries a net positive charge on average, so it moves to the negative electrode.
questions.x: Below its pI, an amino acid has more protons than at neutrality and carries a net positive charge. At pH 3, every glycine has NH₃⁺, and a sizable share still has an un-ionized COOH, so the average net charge is positive and it migrates toward the cathode. It would move toward the anode only above its pI and would stay put at pH 6.0.

questions.q: A mixture of aspartate (pI 2.8), glycine (pI 6.0) and lysine (pI 9.7) undergoes electrophoresis at pH 6.0. What happens?
o: All three move to the anode
Lysine is positive at pH 6.0 and glycine is neutral.
Aspartate moves to the anode, glycine stays, lysine moves to the cathode
Correct: compare pH to each pI; above pI is negative, below pI is positive.
Lysine moves to the anode and aspartate to the cathode
Reverses the charges; lysine is positive and aspartate negative here.
None move, since all are zwitterions
Only glycine is net neutral at pH 6.0.
questions.x: Compare the buffer pH to each pI: if pH is above pI the molecule is negative, if below it is positive, and if equal it is neutral. At pH 6.0, aspartate (pI 2.8) is negative and moves to the anode, glycine (pI 6.0) is neutral and stays put, and lysine (pI 9.7) is positive and moves to the cathode.

questions.q: In rate-zonal centrifugation through a sucrose gradient, particles separate according to sedimentation rate. Why is the run stopped before completion?
o: Sucrose crystallizes if the run continues
Sucrose stays dissolved during centrifugation.
Particles would reverse direction at equilibrium
Particles denser than the gradient keep sinking; they do not reverse.
Longer runs denature all proteins
Time is limited to preserve separation, not to prevent denaturation.
Given enough time, all particles would reach the bottom and the separation would be lost
Correct: rate-zonal separation captures particles mid-migration, separated by size and shape.
questions.x: Rate-zonal centrifugation separates particles by how fast they sediment through a shallow gradient, which depends on size and shape. Particles denser than the gradient keep moving, and given enough time all of them would reach the bottom and pile together. The run is stopped while the particles are still separated into bands at different depths.

questions.q: How does adding a high concentration of ammonium sulfate precipitate proteins?
o: Sulfate covalently cross-links proteins
Salting out is a reversible solubility effect, not covalent.
Salt ions sequester water, reducing protein solvation
Correct: salting out lowers solubility, and proteins precipitate at different salt concentrations.
It denatures proteins by reducing disulfides
Ammonium sulfate is not a reducing agent and usually preserves folding.
It shifts every protein's pI to the buffer pH
Salt does not change a protein's pI.
questions.x: At high concentration, ammonium sulfate ions bind many water molecules, leaving less water to solvate proteins. Protein–protein hydrophobic interactions then dominate and the proteins aggregate and precipitate, which is called salting out. Different proteins precipitate at different salt levels. The effect is reversible and usually preserves the native fold.

questions.q: A crude extract has 200 mg protein and 1000 units of enzyme activity. After a column step, 10 mg protein with 600 units remains. What is the fold purification?
o: Divides 600 units by 100 instead of comparing specific activities (60 vs 5 units/mg).
Correct: specific activity rises from 5 to 60 units/mg, a 12-fold purification.
Uses the protein ratio (200/10) and ignores activity loss.
That is the fractional yield, not the fold purification.
questions.note: Fold purification = new specific activity / original specific activity.
questions.x: Specific activity is activity per mass of protein. It begins at 1000/200 = 5 units/mg and becomes 600/10 = 60 units/mg after the column. Fold purification is the ratio of specific activities, 60/5 = 12. The 20-fold choice uses only the drop in total protein and ignores that 40% of the activity was also lost.

questions.q: Why is size-exclusion chromatography usually placed late in a protein purification scheme?
o: It accepts only small sample volumes, so it follows steps that concentrate the protein
Correct: gel filtration has low load capacity and dilutes samples, suiting final polishing.
It denatures proteins, so it must come last
Gel filtration is gentle and nondenaturing.
It removes salt, which must be present for earlier steps
Desalting is not the main reason for its late placement.
It has the highest capacity of any method
Its capacity is relatively low.
questions.x: Gel filtration has a low loading capacity: the sample must be a small fraction of the column volume, and it dilutes the protein. It is therefore placed late, after higher-capacity steps such as ion exchange or affinity that remove most contaminants and concentrate the sample. It is gentle, so denaturation is not a reason for its place in the order.

questions.q: His-tagged protein eluted from Ni²⁺–NTA shows a target band plus a few contaminants of different size. Which next step best removes them while keeping the protein native?
o: SDS-PAGE followed by gel extraction
SDS denatures the protein.
Size-exclusion chromatography
Correct: contaminants of different size separate by gel filtration under native conditions.
A second identical Ni²⁺–NTA column under the same conditions
Contaminants that co-purified once will likely co-purify again.
Boiling the sample to precipitate contaminants
Boiling would likely denature the target protein too.
questions.x: Gel filtration separates proteins by size under native conditions, so it is ideal for removing contaminants of different size left after an affinity step. Repeating the same Ni²⁺–NTA column would likely retain the same contaminants, because they co-purified for a reason. SDS-PAGE and boiling would denature the target protein.

questions.q: A racemic carboxylic acid is resolved by reacting it with an enantiomerically pure amine. Why does this allow separation?
o: It converts one enantiomer into the other
Salt formation does not invert stereocenters.
It forms enantiomeric salts with different boiling points
Enantiomers have identical physical properties in an achiral environment.
It destroys one enantiomer selectively
Both enantiomers form salts; neither is destroyed.
It forms diastereomeric salts with different physical properties
Correct: diastereomers differ in solubility, so they can be separated by crystallization.
questions.x: Enantiomers have identical physical properties in an achiral environment, so they cannot be separated directly by crystallization. Reacting a racemic acid with a single enantiomer of a chiral amine produces two diastereomeric salts, (R,R) and (S,R). Diastereomers have different solubilities, so they can be separated by crystallization, then each acid is recovered by acidifying.

questions.q: A neutral organic product is contaminated with a carboxylic acid and an amine. Which wash sequence removes both impurities from the ether solution?
o: Two washes with dilute HCl
HCl removes the amine but leaves the carboxylic acid neutral in ether.
Two washes with brine
Brine dries the organic layer but does not ionize either impurity.
Aqueous NaHCO₃ only
Bicarbonate removes the acid but leaves the amine neutral in ether.
Dilute HCl, then aqueous NaHCO₃
Correct: acid protonates the amine into water, then bicarbonate deprotonates the carboxylic acid into water.
questions.x: A neutral product stays in the ether no matter the wash pH, so impurities are removed by ionizing them. Dilute HCl protonates the amine to a water-soluble ammonium salt, and NaHCO₃ deprotonates the carboxylic acid to a water-soluble carboxylate. Each wash removes only one kind of impurity, so both are needed.

questions.q: A protein of interest precipitates between 40% and 60% ammonium sulfate saturation. Which procedure enriches it?
o: Bring to 60%, keep the supernatant
The target would be in the 60% pellet, not the supernatant.
Bring to 40%, discard the pellet, then bring the supernatant to 60% and keep the pellet
Correct: the first cut removes proteins that precipitate earlier; the second collects the target.
Bring to 40%, keep the pellet
The target is still soluble at 40%.
Bring to 100% and keep the pellet
This precipitates nearly all proteins with little enrichment.
questions.x: Fractional precipitation uses two cuts. Bringing the extract to 40% saturation precipitates proteins that come out earlier while the target stays dissolved, so that pellet is discarded. Raising the supernatant to 60% then precipitates the target, which is collected as the pellet. Going straight to 100% precipitates nearly everything and gives little enrichment.

questions.q: How are (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane and (2S,3R)-2,3-dibromobutane related?
o: They are the same meso compound
Correct: with identical ends, R,S and S,R are superimposable through an internal mirror plane.
They are enantiomers
Inverting both centers of a meso compound gives back the same molecule.
They are a racemic pair
A racemic pair requires chiral molecules; this one is achiral.
They are diastereomers
Both centers changed, and the molecule is symmetric, so they are identical.
questions.note: Trap: R,S vs S,R are enantiomers only when the two ends differ.
questions.x: Inverting every center normally gives the enantiomer, unless the molecule has an internal mirror plane. In 2,3-dibromobutane both stereocenters carry identical substituent sets (H, Br, CH₃ and the other CHBr), so the R,S form is meso, and its mirror image is itself. (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) are therefore one compound, numbered from opposite ends.

questions.q: Which dimethylcyclohexane can adopt a chair conformation with both methyl groups equatorial?
o: trans-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane
Correct: adjacent trans substituents can be one-up/one-down and both equatorial.
cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane
Adjacent cis groups always place one axial and one equatorial.
trans-1,3-Dimethylcyclohexane
For 1,3-substitution, trans forces one axial group.
cis-1,4-Dimethylcyclohexane
For 1,4-substitution, cis forces one axial group.
questions.note: Di-equatorial: cis-1,3; trans-1,2 and trans-1,4.
questions.x: On a chair, adjacent carbons alternate up/down for equatorial positions, so trans-1,2 groups (one up, one down) can both be equatorial.
