For 1,3-substitution the pattern flips, so cis-1,3 is the diequatorial isomer, and for 1,4 it flips back to trans. Cis-1,2, trans-1,3 and cis-1,4 always place one group axial in either chair.

questions.q: A racemic carboxylic acid is treated with an enantiopure (R)-amine to form salts. Why can these salts be separated by crystallization?
o: They are enantiomers with different solubilities
Enantiomers have identical solubilities in achiral solvents.
The amine racemizes the acid
The amine does not change the acid's configuration.
They are diastereomers with different physical properties
Correct: (R,R) and (S,R) salts are not mirror images, so solubilities differ.
Only one enantiomer of the acid reacts
Both enantiomers form salts; the salts simply differ.
questions.note: Resolution works by turning enantiomers into diastereomers.
questions.x: Enantiomers have identical physical properties, so they cannot be separated by crystallization directly. Reacting the racemic acid with one enantiomer of a chiral amine gives (R,R) and (S,R) salts, which are diastereomers, not mirror images. Diastereomers differ in solubility, so they can be crystallized apart, and the pure acids are then recovered with acid.

questions.q: Enantiopure (S)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane is heated in water. What best describes the alcohol formed?
o: An achiral meso alcohol
The product has one stereocenter, so it cannot be meso.
A nearly racemic mixture
Correct: SN1 goes through a planar carbocation attacked from both faces.
Pure (R)-alcohol by inversion
Inversion requires SN2, which a tertiary center cannot undergo.
Pure (S)-alcohol by retention
The planar carbocation erases the original configuration.
questions.x: A tertiary halide in water, a polar protic solvent, reacts by SN1. The leaving group departs first to give a planar sp² carbocation, which water can attack from either face. The original configuration is therefore lost and the alcohol forms nearly racemic. Pure inversion would need SN2, which is blocked at a crowded tertiary carbon.

questions.q: In DMSO, a polar aprotic solvent, which halide ion is the strongest nucleophile?
o: I⁻
I⁻ wins in protic solvents, where small anions are caged by hydrogen bonds.
F⁻
Correct: unsolvated anions follow basicity, and F⁻ is the strongest base of the halides.
Cl⁻
Cl⁻ is a weaker base than F⁻, so it is less nucleophilic in aprotic solvent.
Br⁻
Without hydrogen bonding, nucleophilicity tracks basicity, and Br⁻ is a weak base.
questions.note: Trap: the halide nucleophilicity order reverses between protic and aprotic solvents.
questions.x: Polar aprotic solvents such as DMSO solvate cations well but leave anions free, because they have no O–H or N–H to donate hydrogen bonds. Freed from solvent effects, halide nucleophilicity follows basicity, F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻, so F⁻ is the strongest. The protic-solvent order (I⁻ best) is the trap, since it comes from hydrogen-bond caging.

questions.q: Which atom of a carbonyl group is attacked by nucleophiles?
o: Neither; carbonyls are unreactive
Carbonyls are among the most reactive electrophiles in biochemistry.
The α-carbon
The α-carbon becomes nucleophilic when deprotonated; it is not the electrophile.
The oxygen, which carries a partial negative charge
The electron-rich oxygen is attacked by electrophiles such as H⁺.
The carbon, which carries a partial positive charge
Correct: oxygen's electronegativity polarizes C=O, leaving the carbon electrophilic.
questions.x: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon and pulls the C=O π electrons toward itself, leaving the carbonyl carbon with a partial positive charge. Nucleophiles therefore attack that carbon, and the π electrons shift onto oxygen. The oxygen reacts with electrophiles such as H⁺, and the α-carbon becomes nucleophilic only after it is deprotonated to an enolate.

questions.q: 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane is warmed in water. What is the major alcohol product?
o: 3-Methylbutan-2-ol
Ignores the hydride shift that forms the more stable tertiary carbocation.
2-Methylbutan-2-ol
Correct: the secondary cation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to a tertiary cation before water attacks.
3-Methylbutan-1-ol
No step places OH on a terminal carbon.
2,2-Dimethylpropan-1-ol
A methyl shift here would give a less stable cation, and the skeleton would change.
questions.note: Carbocations rearrange toward greater substitution.
questions.x: Ionizing 2-bromo-3-methylbutane gives a secondary cation at C2. A hydride on the adjacent C3 shifts over, moving the positive charge to C3, which bears two methyls and an ethyl, so it is tertiary and more stable. Water then attacks C3, giving 2-methylbutan-2-ol. 3-Methylbutan-2-ol is the trap: it assumes the cation is captured before it rearranges.

questions.q: A chemist triples [N₃⁻] in a reaction with 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, and the rate stays the same. What does this indicate?
o: That azide is too weak to react
Product still forms; the nucleophile just is not in the rate law.
An E2 mechanism
E2 rate depends on base concentration.
An SN1 mechanism with rate-limiting ionization
Correct: zero-order dependence on nucleophile points to a unimolecular rate-limiting step.
An SN2 mechanism with backside attack
SN2 rate would triple with tripled nucleophile.
questions.x: A rate law includes only the species that take part in or before the rate-limiting step. If tripling azide leaves the rate unchanged, the nucleophile is not involved until after that step, which fits SN1, where the slow step is ionization of the tertiary chloride. SN2 and E2 are both bimolecular, so tripling [N₃⁻] would triple their rates.

questions.q: 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide) reacts extremely slowly by SN2 even though it is primary. Why?
o: Bulky groups on the adjacent carbon block backside attack
Correct: the β tert-butyl group hinders the nucleophile's approach.
It has no hydrogens on the α-carbon
The α-carbon is CH₂; it does have hydrogens.
Its carbocation is too stable
Stability of a cation is irrelevant to SN2, and this cation is primary.
Bromide is a poor leaving group
Bromide is a good leaving group in other primary systems.
questions.x: SN2 needs the nucleophile to reach the back of the C–Br bond. In neopentyl bromide the reacting carbon is primary, but the carbon next to it carries three methyl groups, and they crowd the backside approach, so SN2 is extremely slow. SN1 is also poor here, because ionization would give a highly unstable primary carbocation.

questions.q: S-Adenosylmethionine (SAM) transfers its methyl group to an amine nucleophile. Why is this methyl carbon a good SN2 electrophile?
o: Sulfur is more electronegative than oxygen
Sulfur is less electronegative than oxygen.
The methyl group is a strong nucleophile
The methyl carbon is the electrophile being attacked.
It forms a stable methyl carbocation
Methyl cations are extremely unstable; this transfer is SN2.
It is unhindered and bonded to a positively charged sulfonium leaving group
Correct: a neutral thioether departs easily from the cationic sulfur.
questions.x: In SAM the methyl group is attached to a positively charged sulfonium sulfur. When the nucleophile attacks the methyl carbon, the leaving group departs as a neutral thioether (S-adenosylhomocysteine), a very weak base and so an excellent leaving group. A methyl carbon is also completely unhindered, making it an ideal SN2 electrophile.

questions.q: N,N-Dimethylbenzamide is treated with LiAlH₄, then water. What is the product?
o: Benzaldehyde
LiAlH₄ does not stop at the aldehyde stage with amides.
Benzyl alcohol and dimethylamine
Amide oxygen is lost; the C–N bond survives the reduction.
Benzoic acid
That is hydrolysis, which requires acid or base and water.
N,N-Dimethylbenzylamine
Correct: LiAlH₄ reduces the amide C=O fully to CH₂, giving an amine.
questions.x: Esters are reduced to alcohols because their alkoxide oxygen can leave, but in an amide, nitrogen is a much poorer leaving group. With LiAlH₄ the carbonyl oxygen, bound to aluminum, is expelled instead, giving an iminium ion that a second hydride reduces. The C=O becomes CH₂ and the C–N bond survives, so a tertiary amide gives a tertiary amine.

questions.q: (R)-Butan-2-ol is converted to its tosylate with TsCl and pyridine, then treated with NaBr in DMSO. What is the final product?
o: (S)-Butan-2-ol
The tosylate is displaced by bromide, not hydroxide.
(S)-2-Bromobutane
Correct: tosylation retains configuration (C–O untouched); SN2 then inverts.
Racemic 2-bromobutane
Neither step passes through a carbocation in a polar aprotic solvent.
(R)-2-Bromobutane
Assumes retention in both steps; the SN2 step inverts.
questions.note: Tosylation keeps configuration; the displacement is where inversion happens.
questions.x: TsCl reacts at the alcohol oxygen, forming an O–S bond without breaking the C–O bond, so the tosylate keeps the R configuration. Bromide in polar aprotic DMSO then performs SN2 with backside attack, inverting the carbon. Br has top priority and OTs did too, so the inversion also flips the label to S. Racemization would need a carbocation, which neither step forms.

questions.q: Which hydrogens in pentane-2,4-dione (CH₃COCH₂COCH₃) are the most acidic?
o: All hydrogens are equally acidic
Position relative to the carbonyls makes a large difference.
None; diketones are not acidic
β-Diketones are unusually acidic carbon acids.
The terminal CH₃ hydrogens
These are next to only one carbonyl (pKa ≈ 20).
The CH₂ hydrogens between the two carbonyls
Correct: the carbanion is delocalized over both carbonyls (pKa ≈ 9).
questions.x: The CH₂ between the two carbonyls of a β-diketone is unusually acidic: losing its proton gives a carbanion whose negative charge spreads by resonance onto both oxygens. This extra delocalization lowers the pKa to about 9, compared with about 20 for the terminal CH₃ groups, which are next to only one carbonyl. Acidity depends on position.

questions.q: In a crossed aldol reaction between benzaldehyde and acetone in base, why are few side products formed?
o: Base prevents acetone from self-condensing entirely
Self-condensation is suppressed by the more reactive aldehyde acceptor, not by the base.
Acetone has no α-hydrogens
Acetone has six α-hydrogens and serves as the enolate donor.
Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogens, so it acts only as the electrophile
Correct: only acetone forms an enolate, and benzaldehyde is the better acceptor.
Benzaldehyde is not electrophilic
Aldehydes are good electrophiles; it is the acceptor.
questions.x: A crossed aldol is clean when only one partner can form an enolate. Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogens, so it cannot act as the nucleophile and serves only as an acceptor, and as an aldehyde it is a better electrophile than acetone. Acetone forms the enolate and adds mostly to benzaldehyde rather than to itself, which keeps mixed and self-condensation products low.

questions.q: In an α,β-unsaturated ketone, which carbon other than the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic?
o: The α-carbon
Resonance puts positive character on alternating carbons, skipping α.
The carbonyl oxygen
Oxygen is the electron-rich end of the system.
The β-carbon
Correct: resonance places a partial positive charge on the β-carbon (conjugate addition site).
The γ-carbon only
The γ-carbon is outside the conjugated system.
questions.note: Michael acceptors react at the β-carbon.
questions.x: In an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl, the C=C is conjugated with the C=O, so resonance can push π electrons toward oxygen and leave a positive charge on the β-carbon. Nucleophiles can attack there, called conjugate or 1,4 addition (as in the Michael reaction), as well as at the carbonyl carbon. The α-carbon does not carry positive character in these resonance forms.

questions.q: Which compound is most reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
o: Acetyl chloride
Correct: Cl⁻ is an excellent leaving group and gives little resonance donation.
Acetamide
Amides are the least reactive of these derivatives.
Ethyl acetate
Alkoxide is a poor leaving group and the ester is resonance-stabilized.
Acetic anhydride
Reactive, but carboxylate is a poorer leaving group than chloride.
questions.note: Reactivity: acyl halide > anhydride > thioester > ester > amide > carboxylate.
questions.x: Reactivity toward nucleophilic acyl substitution depends on how electrophilic the carbonyl is and how easily the leaving group departs. Chlorine donates little electron density by resonance, because its 3p orbital overlaps poorly with carbon's 2p, and Cl⁻ is a very weak base and an excellent leaving group. Anhydrides come next, since carboxylate is a weaker leaving group than chloride.

questions.q: Acetic acid is esterified with ¹⁸O-labeled ethanol under acid catalysis. Where does the ¹⁸O label end up?
o: In the ester's carbonyl oxygen
The carbonyl oxygen comes from the acid.
Distributed equally among all oxygens
The alcohol oxygen's C–O bond is never broken.
In the water by-product
Water comes from the acid's OH, not the alcohol's oxygen.
In the ester's alkoxy (C–O–CH₂CH₃) oxygen
Correct: the alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl and is retained; the acid's OH leaves as water.
questions.note: Fischer esterification: the acid loses OH, the alcohol loses only H.
questions.x: In Fischer esterification the alcohol is the nucleophile: its oxygen attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon and stays bonded to its ethyl group throughout. The acid's own OH is protonated and leaves as water. The labeled ¹⁸O therefore ends up as the ester's alkoxy oxygen, and the water by-product is unlabeled. This labeling result showed that the acid loses OH and the alcohol loses only H.

questions.q: Why is base-promoted hydrolysis of an ester (saponification) effectively irreversible?
o: Esters cannot be re-formed from acids under any conditions
Fischer esterification re-forms esters under acid.
The carboxylic acid product is deprotonated to an unreactive carboxylate
Correct: carboxylate is resonance-stabilized and resists alkoxide attack.
The alcohol product evaporates
Volatility is not the reason.
Hydroxide is a catalyst that is regenerated
Hydroxide is consumed stoichiometrically.
questions.x: Hydroxide adds to the ester and expels alkoxide, which first gives a carboxylic acid. In base that acid is deprotonated at once to a carboxylate, a resonance-stabilized anion with no electrophilic carbonyl left, so alkoxide cannot attack it to reverse the reaction. This final acid–base step pulls the equilibrium forward and consumes a full equivalent of hydroxide.

questions.q: Two equivalents of methylamine are needed to convert one equivalent of acetyl chloride fully into N-methylacetamide. Why?
o: The amide must be protonated to form
Amide formation releases, not consumes, a proton.
The first equivalent reduces the acid chloride
Amines do not act as reducing agents here.
Two amines add to each carbonyl
Only one amine becomes part of the amide.
The second equivalent neutralizes the HCl by-product
Correct: otherwise HCl protonates the amine, removing it as a nucleophile.
questions.x: Methylamine attacks acetyl chloride and expels chloride, forming N-methylacetamide and releasing one equivalent of HCl. That HCl reacts at once with any remaining amine to form CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻, and the protonated amine has no lone pair, so it cannot react. A second equivalent of amine, or another base such as pyridine, is therefore needed to take up the acid.

questions.q: Peptide bond hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable, yet peptides persist for years in neutral water. Why?
o: Amide resonance gives a high activation energy
Correct: the reaction is favorable but kinetically very slow without catalysts.
Water cannot act as a nucleophile
Water can add to carbonyls; it is just slow with amides.
Peptide bonds are ionic
Peptide bonds are covalent amide linkages.
Hydrolysis is endergonic at pH 7
Hydrolysis has a negative ΔG; the barrier is the issue.
questions.note: Thermodynamics says if; kinetics says how fast.
questions.x: Thermodynamics and kinetics answer different questions. Peptide hydrolysis has a negative ΔG, but amide resonance stabilizes the C–N bond and makes the carbonyl weakly electrophilic, so the activation energy is very high and uncatalyzed hydrolysis takes years. Proteases speed it by lowering that barrier, but they do not change ΔG.

questions.q: Which acid loses CO₂ most readily on gentle heating?
o: Butanoic acid
Simple acids lack the β-carbonyl needed for easy decarboxylation.
3-Oxobutanoic acid
Correct: β-keto acids decarboxylate through a cyclic six-membered transition state.
Benzoic acid
Aromatic acids are resistant to thermal decarboxylation.
4-Oxopentanoic acid
A γ-keto acid cannot form the cyclic transition state.
questions.x: β-Keto acids decarboxylate easily because the ketone oxygen can accept the carboxyl hydrogen through a cyclic six-membered transition state as CO₂ leaves. This gives an enol that tautomerizes to a ketone, so 3-oxobutanoic acid gives acetone. A simple acid or a γ-keto acid has no carbonyl in the right position to form that ring, so it needs much harsher conditions.

questions.q: Which nitrogen atom is the least basic?
o: The nitrogen of triethylamine
A localized lone pair on an alkylamine is strongly basic.
The nitrogen of ethylamine
A typical alkylamine with pKa of its conjugate acid near 10.7.
The nitrogen of acetamide
Correct: its lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl, so amides are essentially neutral.
The nitrogen of pyridine
Pyridine's sp² lone pair is available, giving modest basicity.
questions.x: A nitrogen is basic only if its lone pair is free to bind a proton. In acetamide the lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl by resonance, so amides are essentially nonbasic (protonated amides have a pKa near 0, and they protonate on oxygen). Pyridine's sp² lone pair is localized but held closer to the nucleus, so it is weakly basic (pKa ≈ 5), still more basic than an amide.

questions.q: Why is pyridine basic while pyrrole is essentially nonbasic?
o: Pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair is part of its aromatic sextet; pyridine's is not
Correct: protonating pyrrole's N would destroy aromaticity.
Pyrrole has no lone pair on nitrogen
Pyrrole's N has a lone pair, but it is used in the π system.
Pyridine is not aromatic
Pyridine is aromatic, with 6 π electrons from its carbons and nitrogen.
Pyridine's nitrogen is sp³ hybridized
Pyridine's nitrogen is sp²; its lone pair lies in the ring plane.
questions.x: In pyrrole, the nitrogen's lone pair occupies a p orbital and supplies two of the six π electrons the ring needs to be aromatic. Protonating it would take those electrons out of the π system and destroy aromaticity, so pyrrole is essentially nonbasic. Pyridine's lone pair is in an sp² orbital in the ring plane, outside the aromatic sextet, so it can accept a proton.

questions.q: Ammonia is treated with one equivalent of bromoethane. A mixture of ethyl-, diethyl- and triethylamine results. Why?
o: Each alkylated amine is at least as nucleophilic as the starting amine
Correct: products compete for the alkyl halide, causing overalkylation.
The C–N bonds rearrange after formation
Product mixtures arise from successive alkylations.
Bromoethane reacts by SN1
Primary halides do not ionize; this is SN2 overalkylation.
Ammonia is not nucleophilic
Ammonia attacks; the products simply compete with it.
questions.x: Alkylating ammonia gives ethylamine, and the added ethyl group makes its nitrogen at least as nucleophilic as ammonia's. The product therefore competes with ammonia for the remaining bromoethane, and further SN2 reactions give diethylamine, triethylamine and even quaternary salts. This overalkylation is why chemists use reductive amination or the Gabriel synthesis to make primary amines cleanly.

questions.q: One-electron reduction of ubiquinone produces which species?
o: A carbocation
Adding an electron cannot create a cation.
A semiquinone radical
Correct: a single electron gives a resonance-stabilized radical intermediate.
Ubiquinol
Ubiquinol requires two electrons and two protons.
A hydroquinone dianion
A dianion needs two added electrons.
questions.x: Quinones can be reduced in two one-electron steps. Adding a single electron to ubiquinone gives the semiquinone, a radical anion (or neutral radical after protonation) whose unpaired electron is spread over the ring and both oxygens. This one-electron intermediate lets Q move between two-electron carriers such as NADH and one-electron carriers such as iron–sulfur clusters and cytochromes.

questions.q: Phenol reacts with Br₂ much faster than benzene does, and substitution occurs at which positions?
o: Randomly at all positions
Resonance donation creates a strong positional preference.
At the carbon bearing OH (ipso)
The OH is not displaced in this reaction.
Ortho and para
Correct: the OH donates electrons by resonance, activating ortho and para positions.
Meta only
Meta direction is typical of electron-withdrawing groups.
questions.x: The OH group donates electron density into the ring through an oxygen lone pair, which makes the ring much more nucleophilic than benzene, so it is strongly activated. In the arenium intermediate formed by ortho or para attack, the positive charge can sit on the carbon bonded to OH, where oxygen's lone pair stabilizes it, so substitution occurs ortho and para. Meta direction is typical of electron-withdrawing groups.

questions.q: Fructofuranose forms when which groups in open-chain fructose react?
o: The C1 hydroxyl and the C2 ketone
Adjacent groups cannot cyclize into a stable ring.
The C6 hydroxyl and the C1 aldehyde
Fructose has no aldehyde; C1 is a CH₂OH.
The C5 hydroxyl and the C2 ketone
Correct: this forms a five-membered ring hemiketal.
The C4 hydroxyl and the C2 ketone
This would give a four-atom ring, too strained to form.
questions.x: A sugar ring forms when one of its own hydroxyl groups attacks the carbonyl carbon. Fructose's carbonyl is the C2 ketone, and attack by the C5 OH makes a ring of C2, C3, C4, C5 and the oxygen, a five-membered furanose that is a hemiketal. Attack by the C6 OH gives the six-membered fructopyranose instead. Hydroxyl groups closer to C2 would form strained three- or four-membered rings.

questions.q: A fatty acid is described as 18:3 cis-Δ9,12,15. What omega class is it?
o: That would require the last double bond at C12.
Uses the first Δ position, counted from the carboxyl end.
Correct: the last double bond starts at C15, which is 18 − 15 = 3 carbons from the methyl end.
Δ numbering counts from the carboxyl carbon; ω counts from the methyl end.
questions.x: Δ numbers count from the carboxyl carbon (C1), while the ω number counts from the methyl end to the nearest double bond. For an 18-carbon chain whose last double bond begins at C15, ω = 18 − 15 = 3, so this is an ω-3 fatty acid (α-linolenic acid). The tempting error is reading the first Δ position (9) as ω, or using Δ15 directly as the ω number.

questions.q: Phospholipase A₂ hydrolyzes a membrane phospholipid. What are the products?
o: Glycerol and three fatty acids
Phospholipids have two fatty acids, and PLA₂ removes only one.
Phosphatidic acid and free choline
That is the action of phospholipase D.
A free fatty acid from the sn-2 position and a lysophospholipid
Correct: PLA₂ cleaves the ester at glycerol C2.
Diacylglycerol and a phosphorylated head group
That is the action of phospholipase C.
questions.x: Phospholipases are named by the bond they cut. PLA₂ hydrolyzes the ester at the sn-2 carbon of glycerol, releasing that fatty acid, often arachidonic acid, the eicosanoid precursor, and leaving a lysophospholipid with one tail. PLC cuts before the phosphate, giving diacylglycerol plus a phosphorylated head group such as IP₃, and PLD cuts after it, giving phosphatidic acid and free choline.

questions.q: Soap molecules (one hydrocarbon tail) form micelles in water, but diacyl phospholipids form bilayers. What best explains the difference?
o: Micelles form only from uncharged molecules
Soaps are charged and readily form micelles.
Single-tailed amphiphiles are cone-shaped; two-tailed ones are roughly cylindrical
Correct: cylinders pack into flat sheets, cones into spheres.
Soaps lack a polar head group
The carboxylate is the polar head of a soap.
Phospholipids are not amphipathic
Phospholipids have polar heads and nonpolar tails.
questions.x: An amphiphile's shape decides how it packs. A soap has a large head and one thin tail, a wedge or cone shape whose tails fit together only in the center of a sphere, so it forms micelles. A diacyl phospholipid's two tails are about as wide as its head, so it is roughly cylindrical and packs side by side into flat bilayers. Both kinds of molecules are amphipathic.

questions.q: Most L-amino acids have the S configuration, but L-cysteine is R. Why?
o: L-Cysteine has the opposite spatial arrangement from other L-amino acids
Its geometry matches other L-amino acids; only the priority order changes.
Disulfide formation inverts the α-carbon
Oxidation of the thiol does not touch the α-carbon.
The sulfur in –CH₂SH gives the side chain higher CIP priority than –COOH
Correct: S (Z = 16) outranks the O atoms on the carboxyl carbon at the first point of difference.
Cysteine's α-carbon is not a stereocenter
It has four different substituents.
questions.note: D/L is about geometry; R/S is about priorities.
questions.x: D/L describes actual geometry compared with glyceraldehyde, while R/S depends on CIP priorities. In most amino acids the priority order is NH₂ > COOH > R > H, which makes L amino acids S. In cysteine the side-chain carbon bears a sulfur, and S (atomic number 16) beats the carboxyl carbon's (O, O, O), so CH₂SH outranks COOH. The geometry is the same, but the label becomes R.

questions.q: Lysine has pKa values of 2.2 (α-COOH), 9.0 (α-NH₃⁺) and 10.5 (side-chain NH₃⁺). What is its pI?
o: Averages all three pKa values.
Averages the carboxyl and side-chain pKa values.
Averages the α-carboxyl and α-amino pKa values, ignoring the basic side chain.
Correct: average the two pKa values flanking the neutral species, (9.0 + 10.5)/2.
questions.x: Find the pI by tracking charge: lysine is +2 below pH 2.2, +1 once the carboxyl loses its proton, and 0 once the α-amino group (9.0) loses its proton. The neutral form exists between pKa 9.0 and 10.5, so pI = (9.0 + 10.5)/2 = 9.75. Averaging the α-groups alone (5.6) ignores the basic side chain, which keeps lysine positive across most of the pH range.

questions.q: A histidine side chain has pKa 6.0. At pH 7.0, approximately what fraction of histidine side chains are protonated?
o: About 9%
Correct: [protonated]/[neutral] = 10⁻¹, so the fraction is 0.1/1.1 ≈ 9%.
About 1%
That would correspond to a pH two units above the pKa.
About 91%
Inverts the ratio; above the pKa most groups are deprotonated.
About 50%
That is true only when pH equals pKa.
questions.x: From Henderson–Hasselbalch, pH − pKa = 7.0 − 6.0 = 1, so [neutral]/[protonated] = 10¹ = 10. For every 10 neutral side chains there is 1 protonated one, so the protonated fraction is 1/(10 + 1) ≈ 9%. Above the pKa the deprotonated form dominates, which is why 91% is the reversed answer. Having both forms near pH 7 makes histidine useful as a catalytic acid or base.

questions.q: In a Strecker synthesis, an aldehyde reacts with NH₃ and HCN, and the aminonitrile is hydrolyzed. What is the stereochemistry of the amino acid product?
o: Racemic
Correct: cyanide adds to the planar imine from either face equally.
Pure L
Without a chiral catalyst or enzyme, there is no facial preference.
Meso
An α-amino acid with one stereocenter cannot be meso.
Pure D
No chiral influence favors D.
questions.x: In the Strecker synthesis, the aldehyde and NH₃ condense to a planar imine (iminium), and cyanide adds to the C=N carbon to create the new α-stereocenter. The two faces of the imine are mirror images, so an achiral reagent attacks both equally, giving a racemic aminonitrile and, after hydrolysis, a racemic amino acid. Getting only L requires an enzyme or a chiral catalyst.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of ATP's terminal phosphoanhydride bond is strongly exergonic. Which factor contributes?
o: Release of energy stored in the adenine ring
The base is not altered during hydrolysis.
Breaking bonds releases energy
Bond breaking costs energy; ΔG reflects the products' greater stability.
Formation of a new phosphoanhydride bond
Hydrolysis breaks, not forms, an anhydride.
Relief of electrostatic repulsion among adjacent negative phosphates
Correct: products are also better resonance-stabilized and hydrated.
questions.note: Trap: breaking a bond never releases energy by itself.
questions.x: Breaking any bond costs energy, so ATP hydrolysis is exergonic only because its products, ADP and Pᵢ, are much more stable than ATP plus water. In ATP, closely spaced negative phosphates repel one another, and splitting them apart relieves that strain. Pᵢ also gains more resonance forms and both products are better solvated, which together give ΔG°′ about −30.5 kJ/mol.

questions.q: Spontaneous deamination of cytosine produces uracil. How does using thymine in DNA help cells repair this damage?
o: Any uracil in DNA can be recognized as damage and removed
Correct: thymine (5-methyluracil) is distinguishable from deaminated cytosine.
Thymine prevents cytosine from deaminating
Thymine does not alter cytosine's reactivity.
Thymine cannot be deaminated
Thymine has no amino group, but this is not the repair logic.
Uracil pairs with guanine more strongly than cytosine
Uracil pairs with adenine, causing mutations if not repaired.
questions.x: Cytosine deaminates spontaneously to uracil fairly often. If DNA normally contained uracil, a repair enzyme could not tell the original U's from damaged C's. Because DNA uses thymine (5-methyluracil) instead, any uracil found in DNA must be damage, and uracil-DNA glycosylase removes it. Unrepaired, U pairs with A, turning a G–C pair into A–T after replication.

questions.q: A chemist must add CH₃MgBr to an ester in a molecule that also has a free OH group. Why must the OH be protected first?
o: The OH would be reduced to an alkane
Grignard reagents do not reduce alcohols to alkanes.
The OH group makes the ester unreactive
The ester remains reactive; the OH consumes the reagent.
The OH would add to the ester first
Intramolecular transesterification is not the main concern.
The acidic OH would protonate and destroy the Grignard reagent
Correct: a silyl ether removes the acidic proton.
questions.x: A Grignard reagent behaves like a carbanion, a very strong base. Any O–H proton in the molecule, here the alcohol at pKa about 16, protonates it immediately to give methane and an alkoxide, which uses up the reagent before it reaches the ester. Converting the OH to a silyl ether removes the acidic proton, so the Grignard adds to the ester, and fluoride later removes the protecting group.

questions.q: Which methyl halide's protons appear farthest downfield in ¹H NMR?
o: CH₃Br
Bromine deshields less than F or Cl.
CH₃F
Correct: fluorine is most electronegative and deshields most strongly.
CH₃Cl
Chlorine is less electronegative than fluorine.
CH₃I
Iodine is least electronegative here, giving the most upfield signal.
questions.x: A proton's chemical shift moves downfield as nearby electronegative atoms pull electron density away from it, which reduces its shielding. Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, so CH₃F protons are farthest downfield (about 4.3 ppm), followed by CH₃Cl (about 3.1), CH₃Br (about 2.7) and CH₃I (about 2.2). The heavier halogens are larger, but electronegativity is what controls the shift.

questions.q: Which type of system can exchange energy, but not matter, with its surroundings?
o: Closed system
Correct: a closed system allows heat and work to cross the boundary but no mass.
Open system
An open system exchanges both matter and energy.
Isolated system
An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy.
Isothermal system
Isothermal describes constant temperature, not what crosses the boundary.
questions.x: Systems are classified by what crosses their boundary. Open systems exchange matter and energy, closed systems exchange only energy (as heat or work), and isolated systems exchange neither. A sealed flask that can be heated is closed. Isothermal is a tempting choice but describes a process condition (constant T), not a type of boundary.

questions.q: According to the third law of thermodynamics, which of the following has an entropy of exactly zero?
o: Any element in its standard state at 25 °C
That condition defines ΔH°f = 0, not S = 0; elements have positive S° at 25 °C.
A perfect crystal of a pure substance at 0 K
Correct: a perfect crystal at absolute zero has only one possible microstate.
An ideal gas at 0 °C
0 °C is 273 K, and gases have large positive entropies.
A pure liquid at its freezing point
A liquid at its freezing point still has substantial molecular disorder.
questions.note: Trap: zero ΔH°f for elements is a convention; zero S applies only to perfect crystals at 0 K.
questions.x: The third law sets an absolute zero of entropy: a perfect crystal of a pure substance at 0 K has a single microstate, so S = k ln 1 = 0. Every real substance above 0 K has positive absolute entropy. The trap is mixing this up with the formation-enthalpy convention, where elements in their standard states are assigned ΔH°f = 0, which says nothing about entropy.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands adiabatically against a constant external pressure. What happens to its temperature?
o: It decreases, because the gas does work with no heat input
Correct: q = 0, so ΔU = w < 0, and an ideal gas's T falls with U.
It stays constant because no heat is exchanged
No heat flow does not mean constant T; the work lowers internal energy.
It increases because the gas occupies more volume
Expansion work removes energy from the gas, so T cannot rise.
It cannot be predicted without the heat capacity
The heat capacity sets the size of ΔT, but the sign is fixed by ΔU = w < 0.
questions.x: Adiabatic means q = 0, so ΔU = w. An expanding gas pushes on its surroundings and does work, making w negative, so ΔU falls; for an ideal gas, lower U means lower T. No heat exchange does not mean constant temperature, because work alone can change internal energy. Heat capacity only sets how big the drop is, not its direction.

questions.q: According to the second law of thermodynamics, every spontaneous process:
o: Increases the entropy of the system
System entropy can fall if the surroundings gain more entropy.
Decreases the enthalpy of the system
Endothermic processes such as ice melting can be spontaneous.
Increases the entropy of the universe
Correct: ΔS_universe > 0 for any spontaneous process.
Increases the total energy of the universe
The first law says the energy of the universe is constant.
questions.x: The second law states that the entropy of the universe (system plus surroundings) increases in every spontaneous process. A system's own entropy can fall, as when water freezes below 0 °C, as long as the heat released raises the surroundings' entropy by more. Spontaneous processes can also be endothermic, so neither system entropy nor enthalpy alone decides spontaneity.

questions.q: Which statement about ΔS of the universe for an idealized reversible process is true?
o: It equals zero
Correct: reversible processes generate no net entropy; system and surroundings changes cancel.
It is always positive
Positive ΔS_universe describes irreversible, spontaneous processes.
It is always negative
A negative ΔS_universe would violate the second law.
It equals ΔH/T of the system
ΔH/T gives the system's ΔS for a reversible change at constant T and P, not the universe's.
questions.x: A reversible process is an idealized limit carried out through equilibrium states, so it generates no new entropy: the system's entropy change is exactly balanced by the surroundings', and ΔS_universe = 0. Real, irreversible spontaneous processes have ΔS_universe > 0. A negative value would mean a process running backward against the second law.

questions.q: Hess's law works because enthalpy is:
o: Always negative for real reactions
Many reactions are endothermic; sign is irrelevant to Hess's law.
Equal to the heat at constant volume
Heat at constant volume is ΔU, and this is not the basis of Hess's law.
A state function
Correct: ΔH depends only on initial and final states, so any path gives the same total.
Independent of the amounts of reactants
ΔH is extensive and scales with the amount reacting.
questions.x: Hess's law says the enthalpy change for an overall reaction equals the sum of the enthalpy changes for any set of steps that add up to it. This works only because H is a state function: ΔH depends on start and end states, not the route. The sign of ΔH is irrelevant, and ΔH does scale with amount, so neither explains the law.

questions.q: Using ΔH°f (kJ/mol): CH₄(g) −75, CO₂(g) −394, H₂O(l) −286, what is ΔH° for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)?
o: Counts only one mole of water.
Subtracts products from reactants instead of reactants from products.
Adds the ΔH°f of CH₄ instead of subtracting it.
questions.note: ΔH°rxn = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants); O₂ contributes zero.
questions.x: ΔH°rxn = ΣnΔH°f(products) − ΣnΔH°f(reactants), and elements in their standard states such as O₂ contribute zero. Products: −394 + 2(−286) = −966 kJ; reactants: −75 kJ. So ΔH° = −966 − (−75) = −891 kJ. Remember to weight each value by its coefficient and subtract the reactant sum, which here makes the answer less negative.

questions.q: Why is the molar enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?
o: Vaporization breaks covalent O–H bonds
Phase changes do not break covalent bonds within molecules.
Vaporization occurs at a higher temperature, and ΔH scales directly with T
Transition enthalpies reflect attractions overcome, not the temperature itself.
Liquid water has stronger hydrogen bonds than ice
Ice has the more complete, ordered hydrogen-bond network.
Vaporization overcomes nearly all hydrogen bonding, while melting disrupts only part of it
Correct: gas-phase molecules are essentially free of intermolecular attractions.
questions.x: Phase changes overcome intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds. Melting only loosens the hydrogen-bond network so molecules can slide past one another, while vaporization must separate molecules almost completely. That is why water's ΔHvap (about 41 kJ/mol) is roughly seven times its ΔHfus (about 6 kJ/mol). Ice actually has the more complete hydrogen-bond network, not weaker bonds.

questions.q: Why are reaction enthalpies estimated from bond energies less accurate than those from ΔH°f values?
o: Bond energies ignore whether bonds are broken or formed
The method explicitly tracks bonds broken and formed.
Bond energies apply only to liquids and solids
Bond energies are defined for gas-phase molecules.
Bond energies include entropy contributions
Bond enthalpies are purely enthalpic quantities.
Tabulated bond energies are averages over many different molecules
Correct: a given bond's strength varies with its molecular environment.
questions.x: Tabulated bond energies are averages: a C–H bond in methane is not exactly as strong as one in ethanol, because neighboring atoms and resonance change bond strength. Formation enthalpies are measured for the specific compounds, so they give exact reaction enthalpies through Hess's law. Bond energies are gas-phase values, which is a further limitation, but averaging is the main source of error.

questions.q: One mole of ice melts reversibly at 0 °C. If ΔH°fus = 6.0 kJ/mol, what is ΔS for the melting?
o: −22 J/(mol·K)
Melting absorbs heat and increases disorder, so ΔS is positive.
+22 J/(mol·K)
Correct: ΔS = q_rev/T = 6000 J ÷ 273 K ≈ +22 J/(mol·K).
Leaves ΔH in kJ while reporting the answer in J.
Undefined, because the temperature does not change
ΔS = q_rev/T uses the constant T, not ΔT.
questions.note: Always use kelvins in ΔS = ΔH/T.
questions.x: At a phase-transition temperature the change is reversible, so ΔS = q_rev/T = ΔHfus/T. Convert kJ to J and °C to K: 6000 J/mol ÷ 273 K ≈ +22 J/(mol·K). The sign is positive because melting absorbs heat and the liquid is more disordered. Leaving ΔH in kJ produces a value a thousand times too small.

questions.q: A hot metal block cools in a cooler room, and the block's entropy decreases. Why is this process still spontaneous?
o: The room gains more entropy than the block loses, because it receives the heat at a lower temperature
Correct: q/T_room > q/T_block, so ΔS_universe > 0.
The entropy of the universe is conserved
Entropy is not conserved; it increases in spontaneous processes.
The first law requires heat to flow from hot to cold
The first law conserves energy but says nothing about direction.
The block's entropy actually increases as it cools
Cooling lowers the block's thermal energy and entropy.
questions.x: Heat q leaves the hot block and enters the cooler room. The block's entropy falls by about q/T_hot, while the room's rises by q/T_cold. Because T_cold is smaller, the room's gain is larger, so ΔS_universe > 0. The first law only says energy is conserved; the second law is what makes heat flow from hot to cold.

questions.q: A protein folds with ΔH = −80 kJ/mol and ΔS = −200 J/(mol·K). Above about what temperature does unfolding become favored?
o: Correct: ΔG = 0 at T = ΔH/ΔS = 80,000/200 = 400 K; above this, −TΔS dominates.
Fails to convert kJ to J.
Inverts the ratio, dividing ΔS by ΔH.
It never unfolds because ΔH < 0
At high T, the positive −TΔS term makes folding unfavorable.
questions.x: Folding releases heat (ΔH < 0) but reduces the chain's conformational freedom (ΔS < 0), so it is favored only at low temperature. ΔG = 0 at T = ΔH/ΔS = 80,000 J ÷ 200 J/K = 400 K; above that, −TΔS dominates and unfolding is favored. A negative ΔH does not guarantee spontaneity at every temperature.

questions.q: A process has ΔG = −50 kJ. What is the maximum non-expansion (useful) work it can perform?
o: Unlimited work, given enough time
The work available is capped by the free energy released.
Equal to |ΔH|, regardless of ΔG
ΔH includes the TΔS energy that is unavailable for work.
50 kJ
Correct: −ΔG is the maximum non-PV work available at constant T and P.
Zero, because ΔG < 0 means all energy is lost as heat
Negative ΔG is exactly what makes useful work possible.
questions.x: At constant temperature and pressure, −ΔG is the maximum non-expansion work a process can deliver, reached only in the reversible limit. Part of ΔH is tied up in the TΔS term and cannot be converted to useful work, so |ΔH| is not the cap. A process with ΔG = −50 kJ can therefore do at most 50 kJ of useful work.

questions.q: A 100 g metal block at 85 °C is placed in 100 g of water at 20 °C. The final temperature is 25 °C. What is the metal's specific heat? (c_water = 4.2 J/(g·°C))
o: Correct: water gains 100 × 4.2 × 5 = 2100 J; metal: 2100 = 100 × c × 60, so c = 0.35.
Assumes the metal has the same specific heat as water.
Uses a metal ΔT of 65 °C (to the water's initial temperature) instead of 60 °C.
Swaps the two temperature changes, using 5 °C for the metal and 60 °C for the water.
questions.note: Heat lost by the hot object = heat gained by the cold one.
questions.x: In an insulated mixing, heat lost by the hot object equals heat gained by the cold one. Water gains 100 × 4.2 × (25 − 20) = 2100 J. The metal cools by 85 − 25 = 60 °C, so 2100 = 100 × c × 60 and c = 0.35 J/(g·°C). Each object's ΔT is measured from its own starting temperature to the shared final temperature.

questions.q: In a coffee-cup calorimetry experiment on an exothermic reaction, some heat escapes to the room. How does this affect the calculated magnitude of ΔH?
o: It is too small
Correct: the measured ΔT is smaller than it should be, so less heat is attributed to the reaction.
It is too large
Lost heat lowers the observed temperature rise, not raises it.
It is unaffected
The calculation uses ΔT, which heat loss reduces.
Its sign is reversed
The solution still warms, so the sign is still negative.
questions.x: The calculation assumes all the reaction's heat warms the solution. If some escapes, the measured ΔT is smaller, so q = mcΔT underestimates the heat released, and the computed |ΔH| comes out too small. The sign stays negative because the solution still warms. Heat loss in calorimetry nearly always biases magnitudes low.

questions.q: When 0.020 mol of a solute dissolves in 100 g of solution (c ≈ 4.0 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises 5.0 °C. What is ΔH of solution?
o: +100 kJ/mol
A temperature rise means heat was released, so ΔH is negative.
−2.0 kJ/mol
Reports total heat without dividing by moles.
−10 kJ/mol
Divides by 0.20 mol instead of 0.020 mol.
−100 kJ/mol
Correct: q = 100 × 4.0 × 5.0 = 2.0 kJ released; 2.0 ÷ 0.020 = 100 kJ/mol, exothermic.
questions.x: Heat absorbed by the solution is q = mcΔT = 100 × 4.0 × 5.0 = 2000 J = 2.0 kJ. Since the solution warmed, that heat came from the dissolving solute, so ΔH is negative. Per mole: −2.0 kJ ÷ 0.020 mol = −100 kJ/mol. Forgetting to divide by moles gives the total heat, not the molar enthalpy.

questions.q: How much heat converts 36 g of ice at 0 °C into liquid water at 10 °C? (ΔHfus = 6.0 kJ/mol; c = 4.2 J/(g·°C))
o: 12 kJ
Includes melting but omits warming the liquid.
About 13.5 kJ
Correct: melting 2.0 mol takes 12 kJ; warming takes 36 × 4.2 × 10 ≈ 1.5 kJ; total ≈ 13.5 kJ.
About 1.5 kJ
Includes warming but omits melting.
About 7.5 kJ
Uses 1 mol instead of 2 mol for the melting step.
questions.x: Heating through a phase change is done in segments. Melting: 36 g ÷ 18 g/mol = 2.0 mol × 6.0 kJ/mol = 12 kJ, with no temperature change. Warming the liquid: 36 × 4.2 × 10 ≈ 1.5 kJ. Total ≈ 13.5 kJ. Notice that melting needs far more energy than warming the water by 10 °C.

questions.q: A gas sample is held at a temperature below its triple-point temperature, and the pressure is raised steadily. Which phase change occurs?
o: Deposition (gas to solid)
Correct: below the triple-point temperature, the gas region borders only the solid region.
Condensation (gas to liquid)
The liquid region exists only above the triple-point temperature.
Freezing (liquid to solid)
The sample starts as a gas, not a liquid.
Sublimation (solid to gas)
Raising pressure moves the sample toward the denser phase, not the gas.
questions.x: Below the triple-point temperature, the liquid region of a phase diagram is absent, so a vertical path upward (increasing pressure) goes straight from the gas region into the solid region. Crossing that line is deposition. Condensation to a liquid can only happen at temperatures between the triple point and the critical point.

questions.q: A substance's solid–liquid line has a positive slope. A liquid sample just above its melting point is compressed at constant temperature. What can happen?
o: It vaporizes
Compression favors denser phases, not the gas.
It can freeze, because higher pressure raises the melting point
Correct: a positive slope means the solid is denser, so pressure favors the solid.
It stays liquid because pressure always lowers the melting point
Pressure lowers the melting point only for a negative slope, as in water.
It sublimes
Sublimation goes from solid to gas and needs low pressure.
questions.x: A positive solid–liquid slope means the solid is denser than the liquid, as for most substances. Increasing pressure at constant temperature favors the denser phase, raising the melting point above the current temperature, so the liquid can freeze. Water is the familiar exception, with a negative slope, which is why the 'pressure always lowers melting point' choice fails.

questions.q: Initial rates: [A] 0.10, [B] 0.10 → rate r; [A] 0.20, [B] 0.20 → 8r; [A] 0.10, [B] 0.20 → 2r. What is the rate law?
o: rate = k[A][B]²
Swaps the orders of A and B.
rate = k[A]³
Attributes the entire 8-fold change to A.
rate = k[A][B]
First order in each would give only 4× when both double.
rate = k[A]²[B]
Correct: B alone doubles the rate (first order); doubling both gives 8×, so A contributes 4× (second order).
questions.x: First isolate B: from run 1 to run 3 only [B] doubles and the rate doubles, so B is first order. From run 1 to run 2 both double and the rate rises 8-fold; B accounts for 2×, so A must account for 4×, making A second order. Rate = k[A]²[B]. Assigning the whole 8× to A ignores B's contribution.

questions.q: Mechanism: Step 1 (slow) NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO; Step 2 (fast) NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂. What is the rate law?
o: rate = k[NO₂][CO]
Uses the overall equation instead of the slow step.
rate = k[NO₃][CO]
Uses the fast step and includes an intermediate.
rate = k[NO₂]²[CO]
CO enters only after the rate-determining step.
rate = k[NO₂]²
Correct: the slow first step sets the rate, and it involves two NO₂.
questions.x: The rate-determining (slow) step limits the overall rate, so the observed rate law matches that step's molecularity when it is the first step. Step 1 is a bimolecular collision of two NO₂ molecules, giving rate = k[NO₂]². CO reacts only in the fast second step, after the bottleneck, so it does not appear in the rate law.

questions.q: Mechanism: Step 1 (fast, reversible) 2NO ⇌ N₂O₂; Step 2 (slow) N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2NO₂. What is the observed rate law?
o: rate = k[N₂O₂][O₂]
Contains an intermediate; it must be replaced using step 1.
rate = k[NO]²
Uses only the fast step and ignores the slow step.
rate = k[NO][O₂]
Ignores that step 1 involves two NO molecules.
rate = k[NO]²[O₂]
Correct: rate = k₂[N₂O₂][O₂], and the pre-equilibrium gives [N₂O₂] = K[NO]².
questions.note: Rate laws must contain only reactants (and catalysts), never intermediates.
questions.x: When the slow step involves an intermediate, write its rate law and then replace the intermediate using the fast pre-equilibrium. Here rate = k₂[N₂O₂][O₂], and step 1 gives [N₂O₂] = K[NO]². So rate = k₂K[NO]²[O₂] = k[NO]²[O₂]. Observed rate laws contain only reactants and catalysts, never intermediates.

questions.q: In a two-step mechanism, species X is formed in step 1 and consumed in step 2. X is a(n):
o: Catalyst
A catalyst is consumed first and regenerated later.
Transition state
A transition state is an energy maximum, not a species formed and consumed between steps.
Intermediate
Correct: intermediates are made and then used up, so they are absent from the overall equation.
Final product
A product is not consumed in a later step.
questions.x: An intermediate is produced in one elementary step and consumed in a later one, so it does not appear in the overall equation. A catalyst does the opposite: it is consumed first and regenerated later. A transition state is not a species formed between steps at all; it is the fleeting high-energy arrangement at the top of each barrier.

questions.q: How does the half-life of a zero-order reaction change as the reaction proceeds and [A] falls?
o: It stays constant
Constant half-life is the signature of first order.
Each successive half-life gets longer
That is the pattern for second order.
It always equals 0.693/k
That is the first-order half-life formula.
Each successive half-life gets shorter
Correct: t½ = [A]₀/(2k), so lower starting concentration means shorter half-life.
questions.x: For a zero-order reaction, [A] falls at a constant rate k, so t½ = [A]₀/(2k) is proportional to the starting concentration. Each successive half-life starts from a smaller amount and so is shorter (half as long as the previous one). Only first-order reactions have a constant half-life.

questions.q: A second-order reaction (rate = k[A]²) has a half-life of 20 s when [A]₀ = 0.10 M. What is the half-life when [A]₀ = 0.20 M?
o: Treats the half-life as concentration-independent, as in first order.
Correct: t½ = 1/(k[A]₀), so doubling [A]₀ halves t½.
Applies the zero-order relationship, where t½ ∝ [A]₀.
5 s
Applies an inverse-square dependence that does not exist.
questions.x: For a second-order reaction, t½ = 1/(k[A]₀), so the half-life is inversely proportional to the starting concentration. Doubling [A]₀ from 0.10 M to 0.20 M halves t½ from 20 s to 10 s. Higher concentration means more frequent collisions, so half the reactant is used up faster.

questions.q: Reaction X has a larger activation energy than reaction Y. Both are warmed by 10 K. Which is true?
o: k for X increases by a smaller factor than k for Y
A high-Ea reaction is more, not less, temperature sensitive.
Both k values increase by the same factor
The factor depends on Ea in the exponent.
k for X decreases while k for Y increases
Raising T increases k for any reaction with positive Ea.
k for X increases by a larger factor than k for Y
Correct: a larger Ea makes the rate constant more sensitive to temperature.
questions.x: The temperature sensitivity of k comes from the exponent −Ea/RT: d(ln k)/dT = Ea/(RT²). A reaction with a larger Ea therefore has its rate constant multiplied by a larger factor for the same temperature rise. Every reaction with positive Ea speeds up on heating, but high-barrier reactions speed up most.

questions.q: A catalyst increases the forward rate constant of a reversible reaction 100-fold. By what factor does it change the reverse rate constant?
o: It leaves it unchanged
Then K would increase 100-fold, which a catalyst cannot do.
It increases it 100-fold
Correct: K = k_f/k_r is unchanged, so k_r must rise by the same factor.
It decreases it 100-fold
Then K would increase 10,000-fold.
It increases it 10,000-fold
Then K would decrease, which a catalyst cannot do.
questions.x: For a reversible reaction at equilibrium, K = k_f/k_r. A catalyst cannot change K because it does not change ΔG°, so any increase in k_f must be matched by the same increase in k_r. Raising k_f 100-fold therefore raises k_r 100-fold too, because the same lowered barrier is crossed in both directions.

questions.q: According to the Hammond postulate, the transition state of a highly exothermic elementary step most closely resembles:
o: The products
Product-like transition states occur in endothermic steps.
An intermediate halfway along the coordinate
Highly exothermic steps have early, not midway, transition states.
Neither, because structure is unrelated to energy
Hammond's postulate links similar energy with similar structure.
The reactants
Correct: an early transition state is closer in energy, and structure, to the reactants.
questions.x: The Hammond postulate says a transition state resembles the species closest to it in energy. In a highly exothermic step the transition state is reached early, while it is still close in energy to the reactants, so it is reactant-like in structure. In a strongly endothermic step it comes late and resembles the products.

questions.q: K = 4.0 for A ⇌ 2B. What is K for 4B ⇌ 2A?
o: Reverses the reaction but forgets to square for the doubled coefficients.
Squares K but forgets to invert it for the reverse direction.
Correct: reverse gives 1/4; doubling squares it: (1/4)² = 1/16 = 0.0625.
Multiplies 1/K by ½ instead of squaring it.
questions.note: Reverse → 1/K; multiply coefficients by n → Kⁿ.
questions.x: Two rules: reversing a reaction inverts K, and multiplying all coefficients by n raises K to the nth power. 4B ⇌ 2A is the reverse of A ⇌ 2B, doubled. So K = (1/4.0)² = 1/16 = 0.0625. Inverting without squaring gives 0.25, the most tempting partial answer.

questions.q: Argon is added to a rigid, fixed-volume vessel containing PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) at equilibrium. What happens?
o: A shift toward PCl₅, because the total pressure increased
Total pressure rises, but each reacting gas's partial pressure is unchanged.
A shift toward PCl₃ and Cl₂
Nothing has lowered Q below K.
K decreases
K depends only on temperature.
No shift, because the partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged
Correct: at constant volume, an inert gas does not change Q.
questions.note: Inert gas at constant V: no shift. At constant P (volume grows): shift toward more moles.
questions.x: Adding an inert gas at constant volume raises the total pressure but leaves the moles and volume of each reacting gas, and so their partial pressures and concentrations, unchanged. Q still equals K, so there is no shift. If the argon were added at constant total pressure, the volume would grow and the equilibrium would shift toward the side with more gas moles.

questions.q: Product P1 forms with Ea = 50 kJ/mol (ΔG° = −10 kJ/mol) and P2 with Ea = 80 kJ/mol (ΔG° = −40 kJ/mol); both form reversibly. After prolonged heating, which product dominates?
o: P1, because it forms faster
Faster formation matters only when products cannot revert.
P2, because it is lower in free energy
Correct: with reversibility and enough energy, the mixture equilibrates to the more stable product.
Equal amounts, because both pathways are open
Equilibrium ratios depend on relative stability.
Neither; both revert to reactant
Both products are favored over reactant (ΔG° < 0).
questions.x: With prolonged heating and reversible formation, both pathways can run backward, so the mixture equilibrates. At equilibrium, product ratios depend on relative free energies, not barriers. P2 has the more negative ΔG° (−40 vs −10 kJ/mol), so it is the thermodynamic product and dominates. Rate matters only when products are locked in.

questions.q: HBr adds to 1,3-butadiene. At −80 °C the 1,2-adduct is the major product; at 40 °C the 1,4-adduct is major. Which inference is correct?
o: The 1,2-adduct is more stable; the 1,4-adduct forms faster
Reverses the kinetic and thermodynamic roles.
The 1,2-adduct forms faster; the 1,4-adduct is more stable
Correct: low T gives the kinetic product; higher T allows equilibration to the stable one.
Both adducts have the same stability
Different equilibrium outcomes reflect different stabilities.
Temperature changes ΔG° so much that the faster product changes
The barrier order is unchanged; reversibility at high T is what changes.
questions.x: At −80 °C the additions are effectively irreversible, so the product that forms fastest, the 1,2-adduct, dominates: it is the kinetic product. At 40 °C the adducts can revert and interconvert, so the mixture reaches equilibrium and favors the more stable 1,4-adduct with its more substituted double bond. The barriers do not swap; reversibility does the work.
